angle: Anthropic's own official guidance — the Claude Code best-practices and prompting docs, plus the "How Anthropic teams use Claude Code" report — on driving a feature from vague idea to shippable work.
summary: Anthropic's official guidance converges on one core idea: structure the work around the model's context window and give Claude a way to verify itself. The recommended feature loop is Explore (plan mode) -> Plan (detailed plan or interview-to-SPEC.md) -> Implement -> Commit/PR, with verifiable success criteria (tests, build, screenshot diff) closing the loop so you can walk away. Anthropic's own teams report concrete patterns: a clean-git + checkpoint "try-and-rollback" prototyping mode, distinguishing async-safe tasks from those needing synchronous oversight, detailed CLAUDE.md files refined at end of each session, sub-agents for research and adversarial review, and treating Claude as an iterative partner rather than a one-shot oracle (the RL team notes one-shot works ~1/3 of the time). A genuine cross-source tension exists: older best-practice advice to add "IMPORTANT/YOU MUST" emphasis now conflicts with Claude 4.6/4.8 guidance to dial that back because newer models over-trigger.

techniques.name: Explore -> Plan -> Code -> Commit (plan mode)
techniques.description: Anthropic's recommended four-phase workflow for non-trivial features. Enter plan mode (Shift+Tab or --permission-mode plan) so Claude reads files and answers questions without editing; ask for a detailed implementation plan (Ctrl+G opens it in your editor to refine); exit plan mode to implement against the plan; then commit. Skip the plan for one-sentence diffs (typos, log lines) where it only adds overhead.
techniques.whenToUse: Research and Plan (and gates the transition into Build)

techniques.name: Give Claude a check it can run
techniques.description: The single highest-leverage practice: provide a pass/fail signal Claude reads in-conversation (test suite, build exit code, linter, fixture diff, or a browser screenshot compared against a design). Without it, 'looks done' is the only signal and you become the verification loop. Escalate the gate as needed: ask it to run the check in one prompt, set a /goal condition, use a Stop hook, or have a verification sub-agent re-check. 'If you can't verify it, don't ship it.'
techniques.whenToUse: Verify (and Build, since the loop closes during implementation)

techniques.name: Provide specific context and reference existing patterns
techniques.description: Precise prompts cut corrections. Scope the task (which file, which scenario, testing prefs), point to sources (git history, a specific file), reference an existing example to follow ('look at HotDogWidget.php and follow the pattern'), and describe a bug as symptom + likely location + what 'fixed' looks like. Feed rich context: @ to reference files, paste/drag screenshots, give doc URLs, or pipe data (cat error.log | claude).

techniques.name: Let Claude interview you into a SPEC.md
techniques.description: For larger features, start minimal and ask Claude to interview you with the AskUserQuestion tool about implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, and tradeoffs, then write a complete spec to SPEC.md. Start a fresh session to execute it. Good specs are self-contained: name the files/interfaces, state what's out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step. Anthropic's Growth Marketing team independently does this: brainstorm/prompt-plan in Claude.ai first, then hand the structured plan to Claude Code.

techniques.name: Write a lean, refined CLAUDE.md (and prune it)
techniques.description: CLAUDE.md loads every session with persistent context Claude can't infer: bash commands, code-style deviations, test runner, repo etiquette, env quirks, gotchas. Run /init to bootstrap. Keep it short — for each line ask 'would removing this cause a mistake?' A bloated file makes Claude ignore rules. Anthropic teams refine it continuously: the Data Infrastructure team asks Claude at end of each session to suggest CLAUDE.md improvements; the RL team adds tool-calling fixes like 'run pytest, don't cd unnecessarily — use the right path.'
techniques.whenToUse: Build (one-time setup that compounds across the whole loop)

techniques.name: Delegate research to sub-agents
techniques.description: Since context is the fundamental constraint, send exploration into a separate context window so only the findings return: 'use a subagent to investigate how our auth system handles token refresh and whether we have existing OAuth utilities to reuse.' Keeps the main conversation clean for implementation. Caveat: newer models (Opus 4.6) over-spawn sub-agents — use a direct grep when that's faster.

techniques.name: Adversarial / Writer-Reviewer review in a fresh context
techniques.description: Before counting work done, have a fresh-context reviewer see only the diff and criteria (not the reasoning that produced it). Run the bundled /code-review skill for bug-finding, or write a prompt to check the diff against PLAN.md ('every requirement implemented, listed edge cases have tests, nothing out of scope changed — report gaps, not style'). Or run a two-session Writer/Reviewer pattern. Caveat: a reviewer asked for gaps will usually find some even when work is sound — tell it to flag only correctness/requirement gaps to avoid over-engineering.

techniques.name: Commit and open the PR via gh
techniques.description: Ask Claude directly ('create a pr for my changes') or guide it: summarize the changes, create the PR, then enhance the description. Install the gh CLI so Claude can open PRs and read comments without hitting unauthenticated rate limits. When you create the PR with gh, the session auto-links to it (resume later with claude --from-pr <number>). Review the generated PR and ask Claude to highlight risks before submitting.

techniques.name: Course-correct early; /clear and checkpoint
techniques.description: Tight feedback loops beat one perfect shot. Stop with Esc (context preserved), Esc+Esc or /rewind to restore prior state, or 'undo that.' After two failed corrections on the same issue, /clear and rewrite a better prompt incorporating what you learned — a clean session almost always beats a long polluted one. Every prompt is a checkpoint, enabling a 'try something risky, rewind if it fails' style. (Checkpoints track only Claude's changes, not a git replacement.)

techniques.name: Clean-git + checkpoint-heavy autonomous prototyping
techniques.description: Anthropic's own product, data-science, and RL teams' pattern: start from a clean git state, enable auto-accept mode, set up an autonomous loop (Claude writes code, runs tests, iterates), let it run, then review the ~80% solution. Commit checkpoints frequently so you can revert if it goes off track ('try and rollback'). The data-science team calls it treating Claude 'like a slot machine' — let it run ~30 min, accept or restart fresh rather than wrestling corrections.

techniques.name: Classify tasks: async-autonomous vs synchronous-supervised
techniques.description: The Claude Code team's intuition: peripheral/abstract features and prototyping work well asynchronously with auto-accept mode; core business logic and critical fixes need synchronous, real-time oversight for quality, style, and architecture. The RL team treats it as supervised autonomy — let Claude lead small-to-medium features but steer when it drifts. Decide the mode before you start.

techniques.name: Treat Claude as an iterative partner, not a one-shot oracle
techniques.description: Anthropic's API Knowledge team: approach Claude as a collaborator you iterate with rather than expecting perfect first-try solutions. The RL team is concrete: try a one-shot prompt first (works ~1/3 of the time, saving big when it does), otherwise switch to a guided collaborative approach. Multi-context-window tip: have Claude write tests in a structured file (tests.json) and track progress notes, then continue from a fresh window using git + filesystem state rather than relying on compaction.

techniques.name: Be explicit to trigger action; add motivation; curb over-engineering
techniques.description: Prompting guidance: Claude follows instructions literally, so 'suggest changes' yields suggestions while 'make these edits' yields edits — be explicit when you want action. Explaining the why behind an instruction improves targeting. For newer models, counter their tendency to over-engineer with guidance to keep changes minimal and scoped, and tell Claude not to hard-code to pass tests but to implement a general solution ('Tests verify correctness, not define the solution').

notableQuotesOrExamples: 'Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare. It's the difference between a session you watch and one you walk away from.' — Best practices for Claude Code
'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.' — on when plan mode is overhead
'For each line, ask: Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes? If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!'

Writer/Reviewer pattern: Session A 'Implement a rate limiter for our API endpoints'; Session B (fresh context) 'Review the rate limiter implementation... Look for edge cases, race conditions, and consistency with our existing middleware patterns.'
Anthropic Data Science team: treat Claude 'like a slot machine — commit their state, let Claude work autonomously for 30 minutes, and either accept the solution or restart fresh if it doesn't work.'

Anthropic RL Engineering team: Claude Code can implement small-to-medium PRs 'with relatively little time' but 'it only works on first attempt about one-third of the time, requiring either additional guidance or manual intervention.'

Model-evolution conflict: best-practices doc says 'add emphasis (e.g., IMPORTANT or YOU MUST) to improve adherence,' while the Claude 4 prompting doc says for newer models 'dial back any aggressive language. Where you might have said CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when..., you can use more normal prompting like Use this tool when...' because they now over-trigger.

Anthropic Product Development team start-clean pattern: enable 'auto-accept mode (shift+tab)', set up autonomous loops, 'review the 80% complete solution before taking over for final refinements,' emphasizing 'starting from a clean git state and committing checkpoints regularly.'

angle: Claude Code best practices: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, project memory, and how teams structure context across the Pick -> Research -> Plan -> Build -> Verify -> Share refinement loop.
summary: Anthropic's official guidance frames almost every Claude Code best practice around a single constraint: context fills fast and performance degrades as it fills, so structuring context deliberately is the core skill. CLAUDE.md is the persistent, version-controlled briefing loaded every session (keep it under ~200 lines, concrete and verifiable, pruned ruthlessly); auto memory lets Claude accumulate learnings itself; .claude/rules/ and skills scope instructions so they load only when relevant. Crucially, CLAUDE.md is delivered as a user message, not the system prompt, so it shapes but does not enforce behavior — hooks are the deterministic layer. For teams and multiple agents, the recommended pattern is one shared source: keep an AGENTS.md baseline (the cross-tool open standard) and have CLAUDE.md import it with @AGENTS.md rather than duplicate, with managed-policy CLAUDE.md for org-wide rules; Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md directly.

techniques.name: Write a tight, verifiable CLAUDE.md and run /init to seed it
techniques.description: CLAUDE.md is read at the start of every session and loaded in full, so it must earn its tokens. Run /init to auto-generate a starter from the codebase (build systems, test frameworks, conventions), then refine with things Claude can't infer. Include: bash commands Claude can't guess, code-style rules that differ from defaults, test runners, repo etiquette (branch naming, PR conventions), project-specific architecture, env quirks, and gotchas. Exclude: anything Claude can read from code, standard language conventions, frequently-changing info, long tutorials, and self-evident advice like 'write clean code'. Write concrete, checkable instructions ('Use 2-space indentation', 'Run npm test before committing'), not vague preferences. Litmus test for each line: 'Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?' If not, cut it.
techniques.whenToUse: Build (setup); applies across all phases since it loads every session

techniques.name: Keep CLAUDE.md small; scope the rest with .claude/rules/ and skills
techniques.description: Target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md — longer files consume context and reduce adherence ('Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions'). For larger projects, split topics into .claude/rules/*.md (code-style.md, testing.md, security.md). Rules with no frontmatter load every session at the same priority as CLAUDE.md; rules with a `paths:` glob (e.g. src/api/**/*.ts) are path-scoped and only enter context when Claude touches matching files. For multi-step procedures or domain knowledge that only matters sometimes, use skills (.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md), which load on demand instead of bloating every conversation. Note: @path imports help organize but do NOT save context — imported files still load at launch.
techniques.whenToUse: Build (setup); path-scoped rules pay off during Build when editing specific subsystems

techniques.name: Understand the load hierarchy and use it for team scope
techniques.description: CLAUDE.md files load broadest-to-most-specific: managed policy (org-wide, IT/DevOps-deployed, cannot be excluded) -> user (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) -> project (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, checked into git for the team) -> local (./CLAUDE.local.md, gitignored personal notes). In monorepos, Claude walks up the tree concatenating files root-down so the closest file is read last; subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load on demand when Claude reads files there. Teams check the project CLAUDE.md into git so everyone contributes and it compounds in value; orgs deploy a managed CLAUDE.md (macOS /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/, Linux /etc/claude-code/, Windows C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\) or set the claudeMd key in managed-settings.json. Use claudeMdExcludes globs to skip other teams' irrelevant CLAUDE.md files.
techniques.whenToUse: Build (team/org setup); enables Share-phase conventions to propagate

techniques.name: Share one source across agents: AGENTS.md baseline + @AGENTS.md import
techniques.description: AGENTS.md is an open, tool-agnostic standard ('a README for agents') adopted by 60k+ projects and supported by Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, VS Code, Claude Code and others, stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. It belongs at the repo root and holds build/test commands, code style, testing and security notes, and commit/PR guidelines. Claude Code does NOT read AGENTS.md directly — the documented pattern is a CLAUDE.md that imports it (`@AGENTS.md`) and appends Claude-specific instructions below, or a symlink if no Claude-specific content is needed. /init in a repo with AGENTS.md (or .cursorrules/.windsurfrules) incorporates it into the generated CLAUDE.md. Practitioner consensus: use AGENTS.md as the universal baseline and CLAUDE.md for Claude-specific additions, importing to avoid duplication; CLAUDE.md adds layered/path-scoped rules and local overrides that AGENTS.md lacks.

techniques.name: Explore-then-plan in plan mode; let Claude interview you into a SPEC.md
techniques.description: Separate research and planning from implementation to avoid solving the wrong problem. Enter plan mode so Claude reads files and answers questions without editing, then ask it to produce a detailed implementation plan (Ctrl+G opens the plan in your editor for direct edits). For larger features, start minimal and tell Claude to interview you with the AskUserQuestion tool about technical implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, and tradeoffs, then write a complete spec to SPEC.md; start a fresh session to execute it with clean context. The best specs name the files and interfaces involved, state what's out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step. Skip planning for small, one-sentence-diff changes — planning adds overhead.

techniques.name: Pull and reference rich context: @-files, MCP, gh CLI, existing patterns
techniques.description: Give Claude precise context rather than making it guess. Reference files with @ (Claude reads them before responding), paste screenshots, give doc URLs (allowlist domains via /permissions), or pipe data (cat error.log | claude). Point Claude at existing patterns ('look at how widgets are implemented; HotDogWidget.php is a good example; follow that pattern'). Use CLI tools — install gh so Claude can read issues and open PRs without hitting unauthenticated rate limits — and connect MCP servers (claude mcp add) to pull features from issue trackers, query databases, or integrate Figma designs. These are the context-efficient ways to bring a backlog item's source material in.

techniques.name: Use subagents to investigate without polluting main context
techniques.description: Because context is the fundamental constraint, delegate codebase research to subagents ('use subagents to investigate how our auth system handles token refresh, and whether we have OAuth utilities to reuse'). They explore in a separate context window and report back summaries, keeping the main conversation clean for implementation. Define reusable specialized subagents in .claude/agents/*.md with their own allowed tools and model. This directly prevents 'the infinite exploration' failure where an unscoped investigation reads hundreds of files and fills context.

techniques.name: Give Claude a check it can run, then add an adversarial review
techniques.description: Claude stops when work 'looks done'; without a runnable check, you become the verification loop. Provide a check that returns pass/fail — tests, build exit code, linter, fixture diff, or a browser screenshot compared to a design — and ask Claude to run it and iterate in the same prompt. Escalate gating as needed: a /goal condition re-checked every turn, or a Stop hook that blocks the turn until a script passes. Then add an independent reviewer: run the bundled /code-review skill or a subagent that sees only the diff and a plan ('review the diff against PLAN.md; report gaps that affect correctness or stated requirements, not style'). Caveat: a reviewer told to find gaps will over-report, leading to over-engineering — scope it to correctness and requirements only.

techniques.name: Capture Share-phase conventions in CLAUDE.md and persist learnings via auto memory / #
techniques.description: Put repository etiquette — branch naming, commit message format, PR conventions — in the version-controlled project CLAUDE.md so commits and PRs come out consistent; then 'commit with a descriptive message and open a PR'. Separately, auto memory (on by default, v2.1.59+) lets Claude write its own notes (build commands, debugging insights, preferences) into ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md, of which the first 200 lines / 25KB load each session; it's machine-local and shared across worktrees of the same repo. When you tell Claude 'remember that the API tests need a local Redis instance' it saves to auto memory; say 'add this to CLAUDE.md' to make it team-shared. Use /memory to audit what's loaded and saved. The trigger for adding to CLAUDE.md: Claude repeats a mistake, a review catches something it should have known, or a new teammate would need the same context.
techniques.whenToUse: Share (and feeding learnings back to the next Pick)

techniques.name: Treat CLAUDE.md as advice, hooks as enforcement; manage context aggressively
techniques.description: Key caveat sources flag explicitly: CLAUDE.md is delivered as a user message after the system prompt, not as part of it — Claude tries to follow it but there's no guaranteed compliance, especially for vague or conflicting rules. For anything that MUST happen (run before every commit, block writes to migrations/), use a PreToolUse or Stop hook (deterministic shell commands at lifecycle events) instead of a CLAUDE.md line; --append-system-prompt is the system-level option for scripts. Manage the context window: /clear between unrelated tasks; after two failed corrections on the same issue, /clear and rewrite the prompt rather than piling on corrections; /compact <instructions> for targeted summarization; and customize compaction in CLAUDE.md ('always preserve the list of modified files and test commands'). Recognize the named failure modes: the kitchen-sink session, correcting over and over, the over-specified CLAUDE.md, the trust-then-verify gap, and infinite exploration.

angle: Spec-driven / plan-first development with Claude: write the spec or plan as a durable artifact, review it, then have Claude execute against it — mapped to the Pick -> Research -> Plan -> Build -> Verify -> Share refinement loop.
summary: Across Anthropic's official Claude Code best-practices doc, the GitHub Spec Kit framework, and three practitioner write-ups, the consensus is to separate research and planning from implementation so Claude doesn't "solve the wrong problem," and to capture the spec/plan as a reviewable markdown artifact that becomes the source of truth for execution and verification. The mature pattern is a chain of documents — spec (what) → plan/tasks (how, in steps) → code — with a human (or fresh-context subagent) review gate between each, and an end-to-end verification check Claude can run itself to close the loop. Sources agree far more than they conflict; the main nuances are when to skip the ceremony entirely (one-sentence diffs, small fixes), where plan files should live (repo vs. ~/.claude), and the caveat that adversarial reviewers over-report gaps and can push toward over-engineering.

techniques.name: Explore-first plan mode (read-only before any edits)
techniques.description: Enter Claude Code's plan mode (Shift+Tab to toggle) so Claude reads files and answers questions without making changes, then ask it to produce a detailed implementation plan. Official doc gives the 4-phase flow: Explore (read the relevant code) → Plan (ask 'What files need to change? What is the flow? Create a plan.') → Implement (switch out of plan mode and execute against the plan) → Commit. Caveat from the same doc: planning adds overhead; 'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.'
techniques.whenToUse: Research and Plan (and Pick — the skip-the-plan rule is the gate that decides whether a backlog item even needs the ceremony)

techniques.name: Let Claude interview you, then write SPEC.md
techniques.description: For larger features, start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to interview you using the AskUserQuestion tool to surface edge cases, UI/UX, and tradeoffs you haven't considered, then 'write a complete spec to SPEC.md.' The doc stresses self-contained specs: name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step that proves the feature works. Then start a fresh session to execute the spec so implementation gets clean context.
techniques.whenToUse: Research and Plan (turning a vague backlog idea into a precise, reviewable artifact)

techniques.name: Three-document chain with a review gate between each (spec → plan → code)
techniques.description: Treat refinement as three sequential markdown documents — the spec says what to build, the plan says in what steps, the code follows the plan — with a human review between every pair. DataCamp's walkthrough (using the Superpowers plugin) frames the gates as catching distinct failure modes: spec review catches scope creep, plan review catches half-finished stubs/TODOs and conflicting patterns, and code review catches plans that break on contact with the first failing test. When contradictions surface mid-build the loop stops and asks, and you edit the spec and regenerate affected tasks.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan and Build (the review gates are the human-control checkpoints across the loop)

techniques.name: Edit the plan before execution; keep plan/spec files in the repo
techniques.description: Read the generated plan carefully before any code is written — it's the cheapest moment to catch missing requirements, reorder steps, or add constraints (press Ctrl+G to open the plan in your editor for direct editing). Practitioners recommend moving plan/spec files out of the default ~/.claude/plans/ and into version control (e.g. _plans/ and _specs/, or Spec Kit's specs/) so they're reviewable across sessions and by non-developers, and so a pinned spec can be reused to recover after errors.

techniques.name: Formal spec→plan→tasks→implement pipeline (GitHub Spec Kit)
techniques.description: Spec Kit makes specs executable artifacts via slash commands inside Claude Code: /speckit.constitution (project principles), /speckit.specify (functional requirements and user stories — be explicit about what and why, not the tech stack yet), /speckit.clarify (questionnaire that surfaces underspecified requirements before planning), /speckit.plan (tech stack and architecture → plan.md, contracts, data models), /speckit.tasks (ordered task breakdown with [P] parallel markers and TDD structure), /speckit.implement. Each phase writes a markdown file the next phase reads; functional 'what' stays separate from technical 'how' until planning.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan and Build (a repeatable, artifact-per-phase pipeline for well-scoped features)

techniques.name: Subagents for parallel research, atomic commits per task on execution
techniques.description: Delegate codebase research to subagents ('use subagents to investigate X' / 'spin up multiple subagents for your research task') so reading many files doesn't fill the main context — one practitioner orchestrated 14 subagents while the main session stayed at ~71% token usage. On execution, scope each task to a single subagent and commit after each task ('each task should only be done by a subagent; after each task do a commit before you continue') to make rollbacks trivial and enable pre-commit validation.

techniques.name: Give Claude a verification check it can run itself
techniques.description: Claude stops when work 'looks done'; without a runnable check you become the verification loop. Provide a check that returns pass/fail — a test suite, build exit code, linter, fixture diff, or a browser screenshot compared to a design — and ask Claude to run it and iterate in the same prompt. The doc's example upgrades 'implement a function that validates email addresses' to a prompt that lists concrete test cases and says 'run the tests after implementing.' Harder gates: a /goal condition re-checked every turn, or a Stop hook that blocks the turn from ending until the check passes. Have Claude show evidence (test output, command run) rather than asserting success.
techniques.whenToUse: Verify (and embedded in Plan — the spec should end with the end-to-end check)

techniques.name: Adversarial review of the diff against the plan, in a fresh context
techniques.description: Before calling work done, have a fresh-context subagent review the diff against PLAN.md — 'check that every requirement is implemented, the listed edge cases have tests, and nothing outside scope changed; report gaps, not style preferences' — or run the bundled /code-review skill for a correctness pass. The reviewer sees only the diff and criteria, not the reasoning that produced it. Important caveat from the doc itself: a reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some even when the work is sound, which leads to over-engineering, so tell it to flag only gaps affecting correctness or stated requirements.

techniques.name: CLAUDE.md as persistent project context (and split-model planning)
techniques.description: Keep a short, pruned CLAUDE.md (generate via /init) holding build/test commands, code style that differs from defaults, and architectural decisions — it loads every session and grounds planning/implementation in current reality; bloated files cause Claude to ignore rules. One practitioner adds a model strategy: use Sonnet for spec/planning (speed) and switch to Opus for implementation (more reliable adherence to a detailed plan), enabling thinking mode for tricky edge cases.
techniques.whenToUse: Research and Plan (foundational context that makes every phase more accurate)

techniques.name: Know when NOT to spec
techniques.description: Spec-driven ceremony is overkill for small bug fixes, single-file changes, or well-defined simple features; it pays off for large refactors, migrations needing external research, and unclear requirements. The official doc concurs: skip the plan when you could describe the diff in one sentence. One real migration took ~45 minutes for 14 tasks vs. an estimated 2-3 days manual — but the resulting PR still 'required additional manual changes,' so treat subagent output as a draft needing human refinement.
techniques.whenToUse: Pick (deciding whether a backlog item warrants the full loop)

Official doc, verbatim: 'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.'
Official doc interview prompt, verbatim ending: 'Keep interviewing until we've covered everything, then write a complete spec to SPEC.md.'

Official doc on self-contained specs (verbatim): 'The most useful specs are self-contained: they name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step that proves the feature works.'
Official doc verification upgrade (verbatim): 'write a validateEmail function. example test cases: user@example.com is true, invalid is false, user@.com is false. run the tests after implementing'

Official doc reviewer caveat (verbatim): 'A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound, because that is what it was asked to do. Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering.'
