angle: Prompt engineering and meta-prompting: using Claude to write and improve its own prompts for refinement and planning tasks.
summary: Anthropic ships first-party meta-prompting tooling: the Metaprompt cookbook and Console "prompt generator" turn a plain task description into a structured prompt template, and the Console "prompt improver" rewrites an existing prompt by adding chain-of-thought, standardizing examples into XML, and fixing structure. The mechanism is consistent across all of them: Claude is fed a long multishot prompt of exemplar prompts (or your draft) and asked to produce a better prompt, which you then iterate on. In agentic/Claude Code work the same idea recurs as "let Claude write its own scaffolding" (interview-me-then-write-SPEC.md, Claude authoring CLAUDE.md/hooks/SKILL.md/subagent prompts) and self-correction chains (draft to review to refine, often via a fresh-context reviewer subagent). A real caveat: auto-generated/improved prompts can embed now-deprecated patterns (prefill on the last turn, "CRITICAL: You MUST" emphasis) that you must strip for current models.

techniques.name: Metaprompt: generate a prompt from a task description (blank-page fix)
techniques.description: Feed Claude a long multishot prompt containing roughly half a dozen exemplar prompts (customer support, semantic comparison, doc Q&A, Socratic tutor, function-calling), plus your own task and optional variable names. Claude returns a structured prompt template with placeholder variables, ordered instructions, and XML-tagged reasoning sections. Embedded design rules worth reusing directly: put lengthy input variables BEFORE the instructions; use a scratchpad/inner-monologue tag for complex tasks; ask for the justification BEFORE the score; keep a minimal, non-overlapping set of input variables. Explicitly a starting point for iteration, not an optimum, and designed for single-turn prompts.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan / Research — when you need to author a reusable refinement or planning prompt (e.g. a spec-writer or backlog-grooming prompt) and don't want to start from a blank page.

techniques.name: Console prompt generator: describe task, Claude writes a production-ready prompt
techniques.description: In the Anthropic Console you describe the task and desired output format and Claude produces an editable, production-ready prompt template that applies role setting, chain-of-thought scratchpads, XML tag structuring, and example inputs/outputs. The generator is itself 'a long prompt that itself uses many of the techniques' it teaches — meta-prompting in the literal sense. Give it detailed task and output-format info for best results.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan / Research — fastest way to bootstrap a strong first-draft prompt for a refinement or classification step in your loop.

techniques.name: Console prompt improver: have Claude rewrite an existing prompt
techniques.description: Paste an existing prompt and Claude refines it via five moves: (1) adds a dedicated chain-of-thought section so it reasons before answering; (2) standardizes examples into consistent XML; (3) enriches examples with aligned CoT reasoning; (4) rewrites for clearer structure and fixes grammar/spelling; (5) (historically) adds an assistant prefill to enforce output format. Reported gains: ~30% accuracy lift on a multilabel classification task and 100% adherence to word-count limits in summarization. Good for porting prompts written for other models, or polishing hand-written ones.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan / Verify — when a refinement or planning prompt underperforms and you want Claude to diagnose and rewrite it rather than tweaking by hand.

techniques.name: Ask Claude to evaluate or generate your few-shot examples
techniques.description: Examples are one of the most reliable steering levers; the docs recommend 3-5 examples that are relevant, diverse (cover edge cases), and wrapped in <example>/<examples> tags. Crucially, you can ask Claude to evaluate your examples for relevance and diversity, or to generate additional ones from your initial set — offloading example-curation to the model. The same applies to thinking: put <thinking> tags inside few-shot examples to demonstrate the reasoning pattern and Claude generalizes it.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan / Research — when building a refinement prompt whose quality hinges on good exemplars (e.g. 'turn this vague ticket into an acceptance-criteria list like these').

techniques.name: Let Claude interview you, then write the spec it will execute
techniques.description: Start a feature with a minimal prompt: 'I want to build [X]. Interview me in detail using the AskUserQuestion tool. Ask about technical implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, concerns, and tradeoffs. Don't ask obvious questions, dig into the hard parts. Keep interviewing until we've covered everything, then write a complete spec to SPEC.md.' Claude surfaces considerations you missed and authors the planning artifact itself. The best specs name files/interfaces, state what's out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step. Then start a fresh session to execute the spec.
techniques.whenToUse: Pick / Research / Plan — turning a vague backlog idea into a precise, self-contained spec; this is meta-prompting because Claude is generating the instructions for the build phase.

techniques.name: Have Claude author its own persistent scaffolding (CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, subagents)
techniques.description: Claude can write the very artifacts that steer its future behavior. Run /init to have Claude generate a starter CLAUDE.md from the codebase, then prune it (litmus test per line: 'would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?' — bloated files get ignored). Claude can also write hooks ('Write a hook that runs eslint after every file edit'), SKILL.md files for on-demand domain knowledge, and subagent definitions. Treat CLAUDE.md like code: review, prune, and test by observing whether behavior actually shifts.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan / Build (setup) — encoding refinement conventions so they persist across sessions instead of being re-prompted each time.

techniques.name: Self-correction chain and fresh-context adversarial reviewer
techniques.description: The most common chaining pattern is self-correction: generate a draft, have Claude review it against explicit criteria, then refine — each step a separate call so you can inspect intermediates. Stronger version: a reviewer in a fresh subagent context sees only the diff and your criteria, not the reasoning that produced the change, so the grader isn't the author. Write the review prompt to name the work, the plan to check against, and what counts as a finding ('Report gaps, not style preferences'). Caveat from the source: a reviewer told to find gaps will report some even when work is sound, driving over-engineering — scope it to correctness/requirements only.
techniques.whenToUse: Verify — using Claude to critique and improve its own output (and the prompts that produced it) before you ship.

techniques.name: Strip deprecated patterns from auto-generated prompts (skeptical caveat)
techniques.description: Conflict between sources: the 2024 prompt improver lists 'prefill the assistant message' as one of its five techniques, but current best-practices docs state prefilled responses on the last assistant turn are unsupported on Claude 4.6+ and return a 400 error (migrate to structured outputs / direct instructions). Similarly, older prompts leaned on emphatic 'CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool' phrasing; the docs now warn this causes overtriggering on 4.5/4.6 models and should be dialed back to normal 'Use this tool when...' phrasing. So prompts Claude writes or improves for you can carry stale patterns — review and prune before reuse.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan / Verify — sanity-check any Claude-generated or Claude-improved prompt against current model guidance before adopting it.

notableQuotesOrExamples: Metaprompt: 'a long multi-shot prompt filled with half a dozen examples of good prompts for solving various tasks' designed to solve the 'blank page problem' — explicitly single-turn and 'not guaranteed to be optimal by any means, so don't be afraid to change it!'

Prompt improver applies chain-of-thought ('a dedicated section for Claude to think through problems systematically'), XML example standardization, example enrichment, rewriting, and prefill addition; reported ~30% accuracy gain on multilabel classification and 100% word-count adherence in summarization.
Prompt generator is 'a long prompt that itself uses many of the techniques' it generates — meta-prompting in the literal sense.
Claude Code interview prompt: 'Interview me in detail using the AskUserQuestion tool... dig into the hard parts I might not have considered... then write a complete spec to SPEC.md.'
CLAUDE.md pruning litmus test: for each line ask 'Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?' If not, cut it — 'Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!'

Conflict: prompt improver suggests adding assistant prefill, but current docs say 'prefilled responses on the last assistant turn are no longer supported' on 4.6+ (400 error); and 'CRITICAL: You MUST' phrasing now causes overtriggering and should be softened to 'Use this tool when...'

angle: Using Claude/LLMs to mine and summarize an existing codebase to understand a feature's blast radius before building.
summary: The official Anthropic guidance frames codebase understanding as the "Explore" phase of an explore-plan-code-commit loop: before any edits, you put Claude Code in plan mode (read-only) and have it traverse the file system, grep, and follow references the way a senior engineer would, rather than relying on a stale RAG index. The single most on-point technique for assessing blast radius is delegating investigation to subagents — isolated Claude instances with their own context window that read many files and return only a summary, keeping your main session clean. Concretely, you ask impact-analysis questions ("what would break if I change this signature? list every caller, grouped by package") and let agentic search trace import chains and call sites. The recurring caveat across the official docs: unscoped "investigate X" prompts cause infinite exploration that fills context, so investigations must be narrowly scoped or pushed into a subagent; and the agent verifies static relationships only, not runtime behavior.

techniques.name: Delegate codebase mining to subagents
techniques.description: A subagent is an isolated Claude instance with its own context window that does the research and returns only the final summary to the parent session. Because reading lots of files to understand blast radius consumes context fast, offloading that exploration to a subagent keeps the main conversation clean for planning/implementation. Invoke explicitly, e.g. 'Use subagents to investigate how our authentication system handles token refresh, and whether we have any existing OAuth utilities I should reuse.'
techniques.whenToUse: Research — mining/summarizing the codebase to scope a feature

techniques.name: Direct impact/blast-radius query (list every caller)
techniques.description: Ask a precise dependency-impact question instead of grepping by hand: 'What would break if I change the signature of the authenticate method on UserService? List every caller across the repo, group them by package, and flag the ones that pass positional arguments.' This surfaces every propagation site so distant modules don't break silently. Variants: 'What files import this function?', 'Which tests depend on this module?', 'What would break if I rename this class?'
techniques.whenToUse: Research → Plan boundary — quantifying the blast radius of a specific change

techniques.name: Explore-first with read-only plan mode
techniques.description: Enter plan mode (read-only) so Claude reads files and answers questions without making changes, separating research from execution to avoid solving the wrong problem. Recommended sequence: explore ('read /src/auth and understand how we handle sessions and login'), then ask for an implementation plan ('I want to add Google OAuth. What files need to change? What's the session flow? Create a plan.'), then implement. Skip planning only when the change is one-sentence-describable.
techniques.whenToUse: Research and Plan — before writing any code

techniques.name: Agentic live search instead of a stale index
techniques.description: Claude navigates a codebase the way an engineer would: it traverses the file system, reads files, uses grep, and follows references across files. Operating on the live codebase (not a pre-built RAG/embedding index) avoids citing outdated function references or deleted modules. Ask it to trace relationships directly: 'Show me all places where we handle user permissions', 'Trace the flow of a [feature] request from API to database.'
techniques.whenToUse: Research — building a grounded mental model of the feature area

techniques.name: LSP / code-intelligence for symbol-level tracing
techniques.description: Add a Language Server Protocol / code-intelligence plugin so Claude can follow a function call to its definition, trace references across files, and distinguish identically named functions — symbol-precise navigation rather than text pattern-matching. This makes the 'list every caller' impact analysis reliable on typed languages.

techniques.name: Layered CLAUDE.md + directory scoping for noise reduction
techniques.description: Use hierarchical CLAUDE.md files (root for high-level overview and gotchas; subdirectory files loaded additively as Claude moves through code) and initialize Claude in the relevant subdirectory rather than the repo root, so exploration focuses on the feature's area while still reaching root context via traversal. For unconventional layouts, keep a markdown codebase map Claude scans before opening files. Run /init to generate a starter CLAUDE.md.
techniques.whenToUse: Setup that pays off in Research — keeps codebase exploration focused

techniques.name: Cross-cutting audit queries to find hidden coupling
techniques.description: Pattern-matching queries reveal structural blast radius that simple caller lists miss: 'Find all places where the presentation layer directly accesses the database', 'Check if any frontend code imports backend modules', 'Scan our data-access layer for N+1 query patterns'. Useful for spotting architecture violations a feature might touch.
techniques.whenToUse: Research — discovering non-obvious coupling and side effects

notableQuotesOrExamples: Impact-analysis prompt (developertoolkit.ai): 'What would break if I change the signature of the authenticate method on UserService? List every caller across the repo, group them by package, and flag the ones that pass positional arguments.'
Subagent investigation prompt (official docs): 'Use subagents to investigate how our authentication system handles token refresh, and whether we have any existing OAuth utilities I should reuse.'
Plan-mode explore prompt (official docs): 'read /src/auth and understand how we handle sessions and login. also look at how we manage environment variables for secrets.'

Official caveat — the 'infinite exploration' failure mode: 'You ask Claude to "investigate" something without scoping it. Claude reads hundreds of files, filling the context. Fix: Scope investigations narrowly or use subagents so the exploration doesn't consume your main context.'
Onboarding-style codebase questions (official docs): 'What edge cases does CustomerOnboardingFlowImpl handle?' and 'Why does this code call foo() instead of bar() on line 333?'

angle: Context engineering for large codebases: retrieval, file selection, and feeding Claude the right context for a feature.
summary: Anthropic's official guidance treats the context window as a finite, precious resource: performance degrades as it fills, so the goal is "the smallest set of high-signal tokens" rather than dumping the repo in. For large codebases Claude Code deliberately uses agentic search (glob -> grep -> read) instead of a pre-built RAG/vector index, favoring precision, freshness, privacy, and zero setup; the model retrieves "just in time" via lightweight identifiers (file paths, queries) rather than pre-loading everything. The practical loop is: scope tightly (subdirectories, .claudeignore, LSP), explore in read-only subagents that return summaries, plan before coding (often via a Claude-authored SPEC.md), curate context with @-references and a lean CLAUDE.md, and manage context aggressively with /clear, context editing, and the memory tool. Caveats matter: grep misses renamed symbols, high-cardinality searches blow up context, and large monorepos with inconsistent naming can burn tokens where semantic prefiltering would help.

techniques.name: Agentic search over RAG (glob -> grep -> read by cost)
techniques.description: Claude Code retrieves files at runtime by chaining tools in order of token cost: glob (near-zero, returns paths) to narrow, grep/ripgrep (lightweight, returns matching lines) to confirm relevance, then read (heavy, ~500-1500 tokens/file) only after the first two confirm a file matters. Anthropic dropped its early RAG + local vector DB because agentic search is simpler and avoids staleness, privacy, and reliability problems; for engineers this means giving exact function/class/symbol names so grep finds them precisely, and triangulating with multiple terms (auth, session, token, middleware) when one fails. Per vadim.blog, Boris Cherny said early Claude Code 'used RAG + a local vector db, but we found pretty quickly that agentic search generally works better.'

techniques.name: Just-in-time retrieval via lightweight identifiers
techniques.description: Rather than pre-loading all relevant data, keep lightweight references (file paths, stored queries, links) and load data dynamically at runtime with tools, so the agent 'assembles understanding layer by layer, maintaining only what's necessary in working memory.' Folder hierarchies, naming conventions, and timestamps act as implicit signals (e.g. test_utils.py in /tests vs src/core_logic/). Caveat from Anthropic: runtime exploration trades speed for token efficiency and needs opinionated tooling to avoid dead-ends.

techniques.name: Scope tightly: subdirectories, .claudeignore, LSP, codebase maps
techniques.description: Initialize Claude in the relevant subdirectory ('Claude works best when scoped to the part of the codebase that's actually relevant'), exclude generated code/build artifacts/deps via .claudeignore version-controlled in .claude/settings.json, and scope test/lint commands per-subdirectory so full-monorepo runs don't time out. Add LSP / a code-intelligence plugin for exact symbol-level navigation (described as one of the highest-value investments for multi-language/C/C++ repos). For unconventional layouts, write a lightweight markdown 'codebase map' listing top-level folders with one-line descriptions.

techniques.name: Read-only exploration subagents that return summaries
techniques.description: Delegate codebase research to subagents running in separate context windows; each explores extensively but returns a condensed summary (Anthropic cites ~1,000-2,000 tokens) instead of raw files, keeping the main conversation clean for implementation. Example prompt: 'Use subagents to investigate how our auth system handles token refresh and whether we have OAuth utilities I should reuse.' Claude Code uses a Haiku-backed Explore subagent for this. Scope investigations narrowly to avoid 'infinite exploration' that reads hundreds of files and fills context.

techniques.name: Explore -> Plan -> Code, with a Claude-authored SPEC.md
techniques.description: Separate research/planning from implementation to avoid solving the wrong problem: use plan mode to read and answer questions without editing, then ask for a written plan before switching to implementation. For larger features, have Claude interview you (AskUserQuestion tool) about implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, and tradeoffs, then write a self-contained SPEC.md that names the files/interfaces involved, states what is out of scope, and ends with an end-to-end verification step. Start a fresh session to execute the spec so implementation gets clean context. Skip planning for one-sentence-diff changes.

techniques.name: Reference existing patterns and exact sources in prompts
techniques.description: Precise prompts cut corrections. Point Claude to concrete files and example patterns ('look at how existing widgets are implemented; HotDogWidget.php is a good example; follow the pattern'), name the symptom + likely location + what 'fixed' looks like for bugs, and direct it to the source that answers a question (e.g. 'look through ExecutionFactory's git history'). Provide rich context via @-file references (Claude reads before responding), pasted screenshots/images, allowlisted doc URLs, or piped data (cat error.log | claude).

techniques.name: Lean, layered CLAUDE.md as persistent context
techniques.description: CLAUDE.md is loaded every session, so keep root files lean (high-level architecture and critical gotchas only) and push local conventions to subdirectory files Claude pulls in on demand; bloated files cause Claude to ignore real instructions. Litmus test per line: 'Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?' Include only what Claude can't infer from code (non-guessable bash commands, non-default style rules, test runners, env quirks, gotchas); exclude anything self-evident or that changes often. Generate a starter with /init, check it into git, prune regularly, and review configs every 3-6 months since rules tuned for older models can constrain newer ones (e.g. a forced single-file-refactor rule).

techniques.name: Manage context aggressively: /clear, /compact, context editing, memory tool
techniques.description: Run /clear between unrelated tasks and after two failed corrections (a clean session with a better prompt beats a long polluted one). Use /compact <instructions> for guided summarization, and Esc+Esc / rewind checkpoints to summarize part of a conversation. On the API/platform, context editing automatically removes stale tool calls/results near the token limit, and the memory tool persists notes/decisions in a file-based store outside the context window. Anthropic reports context editing alone improved agentic-search performance 29%, memory + context editing 39%, and in a 100-turn web-search eval context editing cut token use 84% while completing workflows that would otherwise fail from context exhaustion.

techniques.name: Structured note-taking / persistent NOTES.md for long-horizon work
techniques.description: For tasks spanning many tool calls, have the agent persist progress, architectural decisions, and dependencies to notes outside the context window (Claude Code's to-do lists; custom agents' NOTES.md), giving 'persistent memory with minimal overhead' and letting it retrieve state later without keeping it all in the window.

techniques.name: Give Claude a check it can run, then adversarial review in fresh context
techniques.description: Provide a pass/fail signal (tests, build exit code, linter, output diff, browser screenshot) and explicit verification criteria in the prompt so Claude closes its own loop instead of stopping at 'looks done'; gate harder with a /goal condition or a Stop hook. Then have a separate subagent review the diff in a fresh context against PLAN.md, seeing only the diff and criteria, not the reasoning that produced it (the bundled /code-review skill does this). Caveat: a reviewer told to find gaps will always report some, so instruct it to flag only correctness/requirement gaps to avoid over-engineering.

techniques.name: Know where agentic search fails (caveats)
techniques.description: Per vadim.blog: grep finds only what you name, so renamed symbols (createD1HttpClient -> buildGatewayClient) return nothing where vector embeddings would preserve the semantic link; high-cardinality searches (useState across a React app) return hundreds of matches that are expensive to process or require many refining turns; and large monorepos with inconsistent naming burn context faster than semantic prefiltering would. Mitigations: layer a semantic-search MCP plugin atop agentic search for conceptual queries, and respect the glob->grep->read cost hierarchy. (vadim.blog also cites third-hand stats like ~92% prefix-cache reuse and 4x parallel-call latency gains; treat these as reported, not verified.)

notableQuotesOrExamples: Anthropic's core principle: 'Find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome' — treat context as a precious, finite resource.
Official best-practices framing: 'Claude's context window fills up fast, and performance degrades as it fills' — most best practices follow from this one constraint.
CLAUDE.md litmus test (official docs): for each line ask 'Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?' — 'Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!'

Good vs bad prompt (official docs): instead of 'add a calendar widget', 'look at how existing widgets are implemented on the home page... HotDogWidget.php is a good example. follow the pattern...build from scratch without libraries other than the ones already used in the codebase.'
Interview-to-spec prompt (official docs): 'I want to build [X]. Interview me in detail using the AskUserQuestion tool... then write a complete spec to SPEC.md' — then run it in a fresh session.

Subagent retrieval (official docs): 'Use subagents to investigate how our authentication system handles token refresh, and whether we have any existing OAuth utilities I should reuse.' — returns a summary, not raw files.
Stats from the official context-management blog: context editing alone +29%, memory + context editing +39% on agentic search; context editing cut token use 84% in a 100-turn web-search eval.
Boris Cherny on dropping RAG (reported by vadim.blog): early Claude Code 'used RAG + a local vector db, but we found pretty quickly that agentic search generally works better.'
Cost hierarchy (vadim.blog): glob (near-zero, paths only) -> grep (lightweight lines) -> read (heavy, ~500-1500 tokens/file); read is 'the confirmation step, not discovery.'

Common failure patterns (official docs): the kitchen-sink session, correcting over and over, the over-specified CLAUDE.md, the trust-then-verify gap, the infinite exploration — most fixed by /clear or scoping with subagents.

angle: Subagents and multi-agent workflows for feature development (parallel exploration, delegation, orchestration)
summary: Anthropic's own engineering shows multi-agent orchestration (a lead/orchestrator delegating to parallel subagents) delivers large gains on breadth-first RESEARCH — their multi-agent setup beat single-agent Claude Opus by 90.2% on an internal research eval and cut research time up to ~90% — but they explicitly warn it is a POOR fit for most coding/Build work because "most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research," and it burns ~15x the tokens of a single chat. For a feature-refinement loop this maps cleanly: subagents/agent-teams shine at Research (parallel exploration), Plan (delegation discipline, plan-approval gates), and Verify (multi-lens review, adversarial hypothesis debugging), while Build benefits mainly from file isolation via worktrees rather than true parallel coding. A candid practitioner report corroborates the failure mode: naive multi-agent designs cause context amnesia, redundant re-reading, and token blow-ups unless the orchestrator stays in control and feeds complete context into each subagent's task prompt.

techniques.name: Orchestrator-worker delegation with explicit task contracts
techniques.description: A lead agent decomposes the problem and spawns parallel subagents. Anthropic's hard-won rule: each subagent needs 'an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries.' Vague delegation ('research the semiconductor shortage') caused duplication and misalignment. The practitioner report reinforces this from the failure side: subagents that read shared registries/protocols themselves caused context bloat; the fix was the main agent feeding complete context into each subagent's task prompt and subagents 'never read registries/protocols themselves.'
techniques.whenToUse: Research and Plan — when work splits into independent investigations a lead can fan out and synthesize.

techniques.name: Parallel research subagents (context isolation, 'start broad then narrow')
techniques.description: Spawn separate subagents per area ('Research the authentication, database, and API modules in parallel using separate subagents'); each explores in its own context window and returns only a summary, keeping verbose output out of the main conversation. Anthropic found spawning 3-5 subagents in parallel (and having each call 3+ tools in parallel) cut research time up to ~90% for complex queries, and recommends search strategies that start broad then progressively narrow. Caveat: this works best when research paths don't depend on each other, and many detailed returns can themselves flood the main context.
techniques.whenToUse: Research — breadth-first exploration of an unfamiliar codebase or design space.

techniques.name: Scale agent count and effort to task complexity (start with 3-5)
techniques.description: Embed explicit effort guidelines so the lead doesn't over- or under-spawn: Anthropic's system tells agents 'simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents.' The agent-teams docs echo this: start with 3-5 teammates, aim for 5-6 tasks per teammate, and note diminishing returns — 'three focused teammates often outperform five scattered ones.' The practitioner cautionary tale: 26 autonomous agents produced isolated, un-cross-referenced reports and ran context out in 15-20 minutes.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan — sizing the team and tasks before fan-out.

techniques.name: Define reusable custom subagents (frontmatter: name/description/tools/model)
techniques.description: Subagents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter; only name and description are required. The description drives automatic delegation (add 'use proactively' to encourage it). Restrict tools to enforce constraints (e.g. a read-only code-reviewer gets 'tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash', no Edit/Write) and pick a model per role to control cost ('routing tasks to faster, cheaper models like Haiku'). Built-in Explore (Haiku, read-only) and Plan agents already do fast codebase research in isolated context. Store project subagents in .claude/agents/ and check them into version control so the team shares and improves them.
techniques.whenToUse: All phases — reusable specialists (code-reviewer, debugger, test-runner) you invoke repeatedly.

techniques.name: Verification subagents: code-reviewer, debugger, and parallel multi-lens review
techniques.description: Delegate verification to focused subagents. The docs ship a read-only code-reviewer (runs git diff, checks quality/security/secrets, reports Critical/Warning/Suggestion) and a debugger that does root-cause analysis then a minimal fix. Agent teams can split one PR across independent lenses: 'Spawn three reviewers: one on security, one on performance, one validating test coverage,' so a single reviewer doesn't 'gravitate toward one type of issue at a time.' Subagents can also isolate high-volume ops: 'Use a subagent to run the test suite and report only the failing tests.'
techniques.whenToUse: Verify — review, test triage, and debugging where parallel coverage and context isolation pay off.

techniques.name: Adversarial competing-hypotheses debugging
techniques.description: For an unclear root cause, spawn multiple teammates to investigate different hypotheses and 'talk to each other to try to disprove each other's theories, like a scientific debate,' converging on a findings doc. The docs note sequential investigation 'suffers from anchoring: once one theory is explored, subsequent investigation is biased toward it'; independent investigators actively disproving each other make the surviving theory much more likely to be the real cause.
techniques.whenToUse: Verify (and Research) — diagnosing a bug or risk where a single agent would lock onto the first plausible explanation.

techniques.name: Plan-approval gates and quality hooks for teammates
techniques.description: For risky changes, require a teammate to work in read-only plan mode until the lead approves: 'Spawn an architect teammate... Require plan approval before they make any changes.' The lead approves or rejects with feedback; steer it by giving criteria like 'only approve plans that include test coverage.' Enforce gates programmatically with hooks — TaskCompleted/TeammateIdle hooks exit code 2 to block completion and send feedback, keeping a teammate working until quality bars are met.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan and Verify — gating delegated work before it touches code or merges.

techniques.name: Git worktree isolation for parallel Build
techniques.description: Since real parallel coding risks file collisions, isolate edits with worktrees: 'claude --worktree feature-auth' creates a separate working directory on its own branch, so 'Claude [can be] building a feature in one terminal while fixing a bug in a second.' Subagents can each get a temporary worktree via 'isolation: worktree' frontmatter (auto-cleaned if no changes). Use .worktreeinclude to copy gitignored files like .env into each worktree. This isolates files, not coordination — agent teams' top rule for parallel implementation is still 'break the work so each teammate owns a different set of files.'
techniques.whenToUse: Build — running multiple coding sessions/agents on the same repo without overwrites.

techniques.name: Subagents vs. agent teams vs. forks: pick by coordination need
techniques.description: Three distinct mechanisms. Subagents: own context, report results back to the main agent only, lower token cost — best for focused tasks where only the result matters. Agent teams (experimental, CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1): each teammate is a full independent session that messages others directly and self-claims from a shared task list (file-locked) — best for work needing discussion/challenge, but higher token cost. Forks: a subagent that inherits the full conversation (and prompt cache) so you can try several approaches in parallel from the same starting point without re-explaining context.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan — choosing the orchestration primitive; teams for collaborative Research/Verify, subagents for delegated tasks, forks for cheap parallel attempts.

techniques.name: Dynamic Workflows (generated orchestration scripts)
techniques.description: A newer Claude Code capability where, instead of manually configured teams, Claude 'generates workflows on demand based on the user's objective. The system plans the work, distributes tasks across specialized agents, compares and verifies findings, and iterates until results converge,' aimed at large-scale tasks like widespread-bug investigation, large migrations, and security audits. Resumable, but 'can consume substantially more tokens than a typical Claude Code session.'
techniques.whenToUse: Research/Verify at scale — sweeping investigations or migrations too large to orchestrate by hand.

notableQuotesOrExamples: Anthropic: a 'multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval.'

Key caveat (Anthropic): 'Some domains... are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today. For instance, most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research.' Agents use ~4x the tokens of chat; multi-agent ~15x — so 'multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance.'
Delegation contract (Anthropic): each subagent needs 'an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries.'
Agent-teams docs: 'Three focused teammates often outperform five scattered ones'; start with 3-5 teammates and 'avoid file conflicts — break the work so each teammate owns a different set of files.'
Adversarial debugging prompt (docs): 'Spawn 5 agent teammates to investigate different hypotheses. Have them talk to each other to try to disprove each other's theories, like a scientific debate.'

Practitioner reality check (Ilyas Ibrahim): naive autonomy meant 'even when the agents worked together, they weren't referencing each other's work,' and a 26-agent design 'ran out of context in less than 15-20 minutes'; his conclusion — 'This design works best only if a single agent handles the task. In that case, you don't even need the idea of subagents.'

angle: Plan mode / plan-then-execute patterns in Claude Code and similar agentic coding tools
summary: Claude Code's "plan mode" is a read-only state (toggled with Shift+Tab or `claude --permission-mode plan`) where the agent explores the codebase and drafts an implementation plan before touching any files; you approve once instead of approving dozens of individual edits. Anthropic codifies this as the "Explore -> Plan -> Code -> Commit" workflow, with an explicit heuristic to skip planning only when you could describe the diff in one sentence. A skeptic's reverse-engineering shows the mode is enforced mostly through prompt injection (system reminders) rather than hard tool locks, so it's a discipline/UI convenience more than a security boundary. The highest-leverage complement is giving Claude a runnable verification check so the plan-execute loop can close itself, optionally with an adversarial review subagent grading the diff against the saved plan.

techniques.name: Enter plan mode to separate research from execution
techniques.description: Toggle plan mode (Shift+Tab cycles Normal -> Plan -> Auto-accept; or start with `claude --permission-mode plan`). In plan mode Claude reads files and answers questions but cannot edit, run commands, or modify anything until you approve. This gives you one decision point (approve/reject the strategy) instead of dozens of per-tool approvals, and stops Claude from jumping straight to coding the wrong problem.
techniques.whenToUse: Research and Plan — the entry point of the loop

techniques.name: Explore -> Plan -> Code -> Commit (Anthropic's canonical four-phase loop)
techniques.description: Phase 1 Explore: in plan mode, point Claude at the relevant directories/tests/specs to read without changing. Phase 2 Plan: ask for a detailed plan naming what files change, in what order, and the session flow. Phase 3 Implement: switch out of plan mode and have Claude code against the plan, running tests as it goes. Phase 4 Commit: descriptive commit + PR, so the git history becomes the handoff for the next session.
techniques.whenToUse: Spans the whole loop: Research, Plan, Build, Share

techniques.name: The one-sentence skip rule
techniques.description: Plan mode adds overhead, so don't always use it. Anthropic's heuristic: 'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.' Plan when you're uncertain about the approach, when the change touches multiple files, or when you're unfamiliar with the code. Skip for typos, a log line, or a rename — just ask Claude to do it directly.
techniques.whenToUse: Pick — deciding whether a feature even needs the planning ritual

techniques.name: Edit the plan directly with Ctrl+G before executing
techniques.description: Press Ctrl+G to open Claude's proposed plan in your text editor and edit it directly before Claude proceeds. One practitioner notes this is faster and more precise than describing the changes you want conversationally, and that committing the plan to version control turns it into an architectural decision record. (Note: that same blog cites `plansDirectory` and `defaultMode: plan` settings.json keys that the official docs do not confirm — treat as a single-source claim.)
techniques.whenToUse: Plan — tightening the plan before it becomes code

techniques.name: Let Claude interview you, then write SPEC.md and start fresh
techniques.description: For larger features, start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to interview you using the AskUserQuestion tool about technical implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, and tradeoffs — surfacing decisions you hadn't considered. Have it write a self-contained spec to SPEC.md (named files/interfaces, explicit out-of-scope, an end-to-end verification step), then open a fresh session whose clean context is focused entirely on implementation.
techniques.whenToUse: Research and Plan — for vague/large features at the front of the loop

techniques.name: Give Claude a runnable check so the loop closes itself
techniques.description: A plan only pays off if execution is verifiable. Provide a pass/fail signal Claude can read in-conversation — a test suite, build exit code, linter, a script diffing output against a fixture, or a screenshot compared to a design. Anthropic frames this as the difference between a session you watch and one you walk away from. You can gate harder via a /goal condition or a Stop hook that blocks the turn from ending until the check passes (Claude overrides after 8 consecutive blocks).
techniques.whenToUse: Verify — and Build, by embedding the check in the implementation prompt

techniques.name: Adversarial review of the diff against the plan (fresh subagent)
techniques.description: Before counting work done, have a subagent review the diff in a fresh context that sees only the diff and your criteria, not the reasoning that produced it. Prompt it to check that every requirement in PLAN.md is implemented, listed edge cases have tests, and nothing out of scope changed — reporting gaps, not style preferences. Caveat from the docs: a reviewer asked to find gaps will usually report some even when the work is sound, so tell it to flag only correctness/requirement gaps to avoid over-engineering.
techniques.whenToUse: Verify — independent grading of the executed plan

techniques.name: Know that plan mode is soft-enforced, not a hard lock
techniques.description: A reverse-engineering analysis by Armin Ronacher reports that plan mode is implemented largely through prompt injection — system reminders like 'you MUST NOT make any edits' — rather than technical tool locks, and that the plan is effectively a markdown file Claude writes (and even edits with the file-edit tool) in its plans folder. His takeaway: for experienced users the special UI is 'a custom prompt to give it structure, and some system reminders.' Practical implication: treat plan mode as workflow discipline, not a sandbox/security boundary; for true isolation use sandboxing or scoped --allowedTools.
techniques.whenToUse: Cross-cutting — sets correct expectations before relying on the Plan phase

notableQuotesOrExamples: Anthropic (official docs): 'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.'
Anthropic (official docs): 'Letting Claude jump straight to coding can produce code that solves the wrong problem. Use plan mode to separate exploration from execution.'
Anthropic (official docs): 'Give Claude a check it can run: tests, a build, a screenshot to compare. It's the difference between a session you watch and one you walk away from.'
Anthropic (official docs), interview prompt: 'Interview me in detail using the AskUserQuestion tool... Keep interviewing until we've covered everything, then write a complete spec to SPEC.md.'

Anthropic (official docs), review-vs-plan prompt: 'Use a subagent to review the rate limiter diff against PLAN.md. Check that every requirement is implemented, the listed edge cases have tests, and nothing outside the task's scope changed. Report gaps, not style preferences.'

Armin Ronacher (skeptic): 'A plan in Claude Code is effectively a markdown file that is written into Claude's plans folder by Claude in plan mode' — and the restrictions are 'narrative rather than technical.'

angle: Test-driven and verification-first development with Claude: give the agent a check it can run, have it write tests first, then read failures and iterate the red-to-green loop autonomously.
summary: Anthropic's official guidance frames verification as the core constraint of agentic coding: Claude stops when work "looks done," so without a runnable check (tests, build, linter, screenshot diff) you become the verification loop. TDD is repeatedly called the single strongest pattern because each red-to-green cycle gives Claude unambiguous, external feedback that stays accurate even as context fills—the agent runs the test, reads the failure as a tool result, edits, and re-runs until green. The agent-loop docs make the mechanic concrete: a "fix the failing tests" prompt produces turns where Claude runs npm test, the failures come back as a UserMessage, and Claude iterates until the suite passes. The key caveats: Claude defaults to writing implementation before tests (so you must explicitly demand test-first), a reviewer/test cannot be graded by the same invocation that wrote it (use a fresh subagent or second session), and tests verify only what you wrote tests for—not necessarily what you asked for.

techniques.name: Give Claude a check it can run (close the verification loop)
techniques.description: Provide something that returns a machine-readable pass/fail—a test suite, build exit code, linter, fixture-diff script, or screenshot comparison—and tell Claude to run it and iterate in the same prompt. Per the docs: 'Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and iterates until the check passes.' Without this, 'looks done' is the only signal and you become the verification loop where 'every mistake waits for you to notice it.' Concretely: 'write a validateEmail function. example test cases: user@example.com is true, invalid is false, user@.com is false. run the tests after implementing.'

techniques.name: Provide input/output pairs as verification criteria up front
techniques.description: Instead of a vague spec, hand Claude concrete example cases that become the oracle. The docs contrast 'implement a function that validates email addresses' (before) with a version that lists explicit true/false example cases and ends with 'run the tests after implementing' (after). For specs, the docs add that the most useful specs 'end with an end-to-end verification step that proves the feature works.'

techniques.name: Write a failing test that reproduces the bug, then fix
techniques.description: For bug work, the docs' recommended prompt shape is: describe the symptom, point at the likely location, and instruct 'write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it.' This forces a red state that proves the fix actually addresses the reported behavior rather than a guess.

techniques.name: Run-test → read-failure → edit → re-run loop (the agent loop mechanic)
techniques.description: This is the literal mechanism behind 'Claude writes tests, you read failures.' The agent-loop docs walk through the prompt 'Fix the failing tests in auth.ts': Turn 1 Claude calls Bash to run npm test and 'yields a UserMessage with the output (three failures)'; Turn 2 it reads the source and test files; Turn 3 it edits and re-runs, all tests pass; final turn it reports done. 'Turns continue until Claude produces output with no tool calls.' The test output flowing back as a tool result is what lets the agent self-correct without you.

techniques.name: Explicitly demand test-first—Claude defaults to implementation-first
techniques.description: TDD with Claude requires explicit prompting because Claude naturally writes implementation first then tests, which defeats the point. Practitioner guides phrase the red-phase prompt as roughly 'write a FAILING test for [feature]; do NOT write the implementation yet,' then a separate green-phase prompt to 'implement the minimum code to make these tests pass.' Anthropic's own framing of why this matters: tests are 'an external oracle that stays accurate regardless of how long the session has been running,' whereas without them Claude's only check is its own judgment, which degrades as context fills.

techniques.name: Separate the writer from the certifier (don't let the author grade itself)
techniques.description: A reviewer/verifier should run in a fresh context so it isn't biased by the reasoning that produced the code. The docs describe a Writer/Reviewer split across two sessions and explicitly note 'you can do something similar with tests: have one Claude write tests, then another write code to pass them.' For done-checks, run a verification subagent or the bundled /code-review skill so 'a fresh model try[s] to refute the result, so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it.' Practitioner framing of the same idea: the invocation that writes the code must not be the one that certifies it done.

techniques.name: Gate the stop with a Stop hook or /goal so unattended runs finish correctly
techniques.description: Escalate how hard the check gates completion: in-prompt (run and iterate now), across a session via a /goal condition re-checked every turn, or as a deterministic Stop hook that 'runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes.' Note the safety valve: 'Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks.' Hooks are deterministic where CLAUDE.md is merely advisory—use them 'for actions that must happen every time with zero exceptions.'

techniques.name: Demand evidence, not assertions of success
techniques.description: Have Claude 'show evidence rather than asserting success: the test output, the command it ran and what it returned, or a screenshot of the result.' Reviewing the evidence is faster than re-running verification yourself and works for sessions you weren't watching. This directly counters the named failure mode 'The trust-then-verify gap'—a plausible implementation that doesn't handle edge cases—whose fix is 'Always provide verification (tests, scripts, screenshots). If you can't verify it, don't ship it.'

techniques.name: Let Claude write tests in unfamiliar languages from your described intent
techniques.description: Anthropic's Inference team uses Claude to write test logic when working in a language they don't know well (e.g. Rust): the engineer explains the behavior they want verified and Claude writes the test in the codebase's native language. This lowers the barrier to having a verification oracle in any stack. (Paraphrased from Anthropic's teams write-up; not a verbatim quote.)

techniques.name: Guide via pseudocode then TDD instead of code-first refactor-later
techniques.description: Anthropic's Security Engineering team replaced a 'design doc → janky code → refactor → give up on tests' workflow by asking Claude for pseudocode first, then guiding it through test-driven development with periodic check-ins, yielding more reliable, testable code. (Paraphrased from Anthropic's teams write-up; not a verbatim quote.)

notableQuotesOrExamples: From the best-practices doc (verbatim): 'Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, "looks done" is the only signal available, and you become the verification loop: every mistake waits for you to notice it.'
From the best-practices doc (verbatim): 'Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and iterates until the check passes.'

Best-practices verification-criteria example (verbatim): 'write a validateEmail function. example test cases: user@example.com is true, invalid is false, user@.com is false. run the tests after implementing'
Best-practices bug example (verbatim): 'write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it'

Agent-loop doc (verbatim), the read-failures mechanic: Claude 'calls Bash to run npm test... then yields a UserMessage with the output (three failures)' and 'Turns continue until Claude produces output with no tool calls.'
Best-practices doc (verbatim) on writer/reviewer for tests: 'have one Claude write tests, then another write code to pass them.'

Best-practices doc (verbatim) on Stop-hook gating: a Stop hook 'runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes. Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks.'
