angle: Extracting architecture and ADRs from code/docs with LLMs
summary: Practitioners use LLMs (especially Claude Code) in two complementary ways: (1) extracting a navigable architecture overview from existing code — C4 models, dependency graphs, mermaid/PlantUML diagrams — and (2) extracting and maintaining Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) by scanning the codebase against a template, capturing decisions during sessions, and consulting relevant ADRs before planning new work. The recurring pattern is structured extraction (clean symbol maps or AST graphs rather than raw code dumps), a template-plus-index file layout, and a tiered/selective reading strategy to keep LLM context lean. Every source insists the output is a starting point that requires human review: AI gets structure right but doesn't know team intent, and diagrams typically need several correction iterations.

techniques.name: Scan the codebase for high-priority ADRs against a template
techniques.description: Point Claude at your repo with a short instruction referencing two files: a template.md (e.g. Michael Nygard's standard ADR format) and an overview.md that defines the naming pattern and acts as an index. The author's actual prompt was roughly: scan the code base for high-priority ADRs using template.md, creating each record in /ADR/records using the pattern in overview.md. Effective extraction needs clear folder structure, template references, and naming conventions rather than long explanations. Caveat: the initial scan generates many records, so you must selectively filter for the ones worth keeping.
techniques.whenToUse: Share (retroactively documenting an existing feature/system) and Research (understanding why current code is the way it is)

techniques.name: Capture decisions during a session with a /record-adr command
techniques.description: Use a Claude Code skill invoked as /record-adr followed by a plain-language decision (e.g. going with PostgreSQL instead of MongoDB for the user service because of transactional guarantees). The skill asks clarifying questions about alternatives and consequences when context is incomplete, then writes a sequentially numbered file into docs/architecture/adr/ and updates a table-of-contents/decisions file. It enforces a fixed template: single-sentence decision statement, considered options with pros/cons, separate positive and negative consequences, and references. Takes about 30 seconds to a minute, low enough friction to do every time. After 5-10 ADRs accumulate, ask Claude to summarize them into a higher-level solution-strategy section.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan and Share — record the decision at the moment it's made during refinement, then roll up into narrative architecture docs

techniques.name: Tiered reading: minimal CLAUDE.md index + selective /adr load
techniques.description: Keep an /adr/ directory of numbered markdown files (001-package-management.md, 002-..., each with Context/Decision/Consequences/Usage). List them by number and topic in CLAUDE.md, keeping that entry file tiny (the author targets under 2KB) so it doesn't burn tokens. A custom /adr command then instructs Claude to consult the ADR list, read only the relevant ADRs before planning a task, include ADR creation/update tasks in the plan, and confirm before adding a new ADR. This prevents loading irrelevant docs while ensuring decisions land in the permanent record.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan — load just the ADRs relevant to the feature before producing the implementation plan, and bake ADR updates into that plan

techniques.name: Standing rule: auto-create an ADR when architecture changes
techniques.description: Add a persistent instruction to the agent configuration along the lines of: always create an ADR when changes affect the overall architecture. This shifts ADR creation from retrospective manual work to automatic capture while context is still fresh, complementing the on-demand /record-adr flow.
techniques.whenToUse: Build — capture the decision as the change is implemented

techniques.name: Structured extraction over raw code for architecture overviews
techniques.description: For deriving a system overview, feed the LLM structured signals rather than dumping raw files: an AST-derived semantic graph of classes/annotations/dependencies, or a tool's repository map that summarizes structure without loading every file. LLMs then output abstraction-appropriate diagrams (C4 system context / container / component levels, dependency graphs) as images, mermaid, or PlantUML. This beats pure static analysis, which produces unusable 500-node diagrams with no useful abstraction, and beats raw-code dumping which overflows context.
techniques.whenToUse: Research — build a mental model of an unfamiliar feature area before refining it

techniques.name: Iterative diagram refinement with explicit correction prompts
techniques.description: Generate a C4/PlantUML diagram with a first prompt, then refine across several passes pointing out specific gaps: try harder and use the Python code; include these files; you missed component overture.py; add streamlit_app.py. The author produced five versions in about five minutes. Expect the LLM to confuse diagram levels (it labeled a Component diagram as a Container diagram, needing a manual fix to PlantUML include statements). Treat the result as a starting point to finalize yourself.
techniques.whenToUse: Research and Verify — iterate the extracted diagram against the real code until it matches

techniques.name: Mandatory human review against team intent
techniques.description: Every source stresses the extraction is a draft, not ground truth. AI gets structure right but naming can be awkward and it doesn't know your team's intent or mental model, so output must be validated by domain experts. Diagrams need human review, always. ADRs remain the human-supplied layer that explains the why behind structural choices that source code can't reveal.
techniques.whenToUse: Verify — gate the LLM-extracted architecture/ADRs on human review before treating them as authoritative

notableQuotesOrExamples: Author's ADR-scan prompt to Claude: 'I want to scan my code base for high-priority ADR using the template described in template.md. Each individual ADR record should be created in folder /ADR/records using the pattern described in overview.md.' (adolfi.dev)
Standing agent instruction: 'Always create an ADR when changes are made to the codebase that affect the overall architecture.' (adolfi.dev)
The /adr command instruction (7tonshark): 'Consult CLAUDE.md for the list of current ADRs... Before planning this task, read any relevant ADRs... If this plan requires a new ADR, confirm with me.'

Example /record-adr usage (beyondautocomplete): 'We're going with PostgreSQL instead of MongoDB for the user service because we need strong transactional guarantees' — the skill then asks clarifying questions and writes a numbered file to docs/architecture/adr/.
First diagram prompt (heuel.org): 'create a C4 diagram for the architecture in PlantUML', refined with 'Please try harder and use the Python code'; five versions in ~5 minutes, last still imperfect.
Human-review caveat (dev.to): 'Generated diagrams need human review. Always. The AI gets structure right... But naming might be awkward.' and the AI 'doesn't know your team's intent or mental model.'

angle: AI-assisted refinement and grooming of JIRA/backlog tickets — turning vague tickets into actionable, well-formed work — mapped onto the Pick → Research → Plan → Build → Verify → Share loop.
summary: Practitioners use Claude (via Claude Code + the Atlassian/Jira MCP) to groom backlogs in two passes: a coarse triage pass that audits the whole backlog for missing descriptions, duplicates, stale items, and hidden thematic clusters, then a per-ticket refinement pass that rewrites implementation-titled tasks into user-centered stories with explicit acceptance criteria and business value. For deeper feature refinement, the dominant pattern is a Research → Plan → Implement → Validate loop where Claude first reads the ticket and the actual codebase, then produces a phased, independently-verifiable plan before writing code — Anthropic's own teams advise "thoroughly brainstorm and prompt plan before coding." Across every source the consistent caveat is that Claude drafts fast but is not always right: bulk actions need a confirmation gate and a human must review acceptance criteria and priority before anything is written back to Jira.

techniques.name: Whole-backlog audit (triage before refining)
techniques.description: Point Claude at the backlog and ask it to diagnose systemic problems — tickets lacking descriptions, items that are implementation-focused rather than outcome-focused, missing epic/hierarchy structure, stale tickets. One PO had Claude surface that '90% of items were implementation-focused' and 'many tickets lacked descriptions', replacing weeks of manual review. Use JQL-style natural-language queries like 'find tickets in ENG labeled tech-debt sitting in the backlog more than 30 days' to surface what to groom first.

techniques.name: Thematic clustering and auto-linking
techniques.description: Claude detects relationships across tickets without being told the taxonomy, then proposes epic groupings — e.g. SAML integration and MFA UI both rolling up to 'Authentication', invoice APIs to 'Unified Billing'. Turns a flat task list into a navigable product hierarchy so refinement happens per-theme instead of per-orphan-ticket.

techniques.name: Story reformatting with acceptance criteria
techniques.description: The core grooming move: convert an implementation-titled task into a user-centered narrative plus checkbox acceptance criteria and a business-value statement. Before: '[BE] Implement approval of free trial requests'. After: 'As a sales team member, I want to approve/reject requests... so that I can onboard qualified prospects', with explicit criteria. Pair with epic-level goal statements and success metrics (e.g. '95% login success rate').

techniques.name: Exemplar-as-template normalization
techniques.description: Standardize poorly-defined tickets by anchoring on a good one: 'Look at how ENG-123 is written and use that as a template for these 5 tickets.' Drives consistent structure (description, criteria, fields) across grouped backlog items without restating your conventions each time.

techniques.name: Read-the-ticket-against-the-code refinement
techniques.description: Because Claude Code sees both the Jira ticket and the actual repo, you can cross-reference acceptance criteria against real implementation. Workflow: 'Show me details for ENG-456' (get_issue) → 'Based on this ticket, what files do we need to modify?' Claude reads existing code patterns and grounds the refined scope in reality rather than guesses. Favor specific prompts ('users logged out after 5 min instead of 30') over vague ones ('fix the bug').

techniques.name: Brainstorm and prompt-plan before coding
techniques.description: Anthropic's own teams advise spending significant time upfront with Claude to think through the entire workflow, then having Claude produce a comprehensive prompt and code structure for Claude Code to reference — and working step-by-step rather than asking for one-shot solutions, to keep it from going off the rails on complex requirements. This is the bridge from a refined ticket to executable work.

techniques.name: Research → Plan → Implement → Validate loop with persisted artifacts
techniques.description: Split refinement-to-delivery into custom commands: a research phase that maps the relevant code (file paths, line numbers, patterns) and writes findings to disk; a planning phase that turns research into a phased plan with independently-verifiable success criteria; implementation phase-by-phase with stops on blockers; and a validation phase (build/tests/types) producing a reviewable report. Plans/research persist in a thoughts/ directory so context compounds across sessions. Specificity is the lever: not 'add caching' but 'add a Redis cache for the product API, 5-min TTL, invalidate on update, fall back to DB on miss.'

techniques.name: Persistent-backlog polish loop
techniques.description: Anthropic teams run a standing 'bug-fixing and feature refinement workflow for their persistent backlog of polish tasks' — treating the backlog as a queue Claude continuously chips at, not a one-time cleanup. Useful framing for keeping a backlog groomed over time rather than in a single heroic session.

techniques.name: Write back to Jira on completion
techniques.description: Close the loop without leaving the terminal: 'Add a comment to ENG-456 with implementation details, then transition to In Review.' Claude both comments and transitions status via MCP, so the refined ticket reflects what actually shipped.

techniques.name: Confirmation gate on bulk actions
techniques.description: Before any bulk grooming op (mass field updates, status moves, consolidations), have Claude show exactly what it will do and confirm first. The recurring caveat across every source: 'AI is fast, not always right — review everything.' Never let automation rewrite acceptance criteria or priority (business decisions) without human sign-off; treat Claude's output as drafts.

notableQuotesOrExamples: Before/after grooming: '[BE] Implement approval of free trial requests' → 'As a sales team member, I want to approve/reject requests... so that I can onboard qualified prospects' (+ acceptance criteria + business value). (daniel-inka.medium.com)
Skeptic's anchor — the one line every source agrees on: 'AI is fast, not always right. Review everything.' (daniel-inka.medium.com)
Backlog audit verdict Claude produced: '90% of items were implementation-focused', 'no Epics or product hierarchy', 'many tickets lacked descriptions'. (daniel-inka.medium.com)

Anthropic teams' advice: 'Thoroughly brainstorm and prompt plan before coding' — spend time upfront in Claude.ai to think through the whole workflow, then have it create a comprehensive prompt and code structure for Claude Code to reference. (Anthropic PDF)
Anthropic teams run a 'bug-fixing and feature refinement workflow for their persistent backlog of polish tasks.' (Anthropic PDF)

Specificity in planning: not 'Add caching to improve performance' but 'Add a Redis caching layer for the product API with 5-minute TTL, invalidation on update, and fallback to database on cache miss.' (alexkurkin.com)
Bulk-grooming safety prompt: 'ask Claude to show you what it's about to do before actually moving them. I'll confirm.' (mindstudio.ai)
Refinement-against-code prompt chain: 'Show me the details for ENG-456' → 'Based on this ticket, what files do we need to modify?' (builder.io)

angle: Mining Confluence and internal documentation with AI to gather context for a feature
summary: Connecting Claude to Confluence/Jira via the Atlassian MCP server (or community servers like sooperset/mcp-atlassian) turns scattered internal docs into a queryable knowledge source Claude can mine on demand. The recurring practitioner pattern is search-then-fetch: run a CQL/JQL search to find candidate pages and issues, then pull full content (and crucially page comments, where tribal knowledge lives) only for the relevant ones — a just-in-time retrieval style that Anthropic's own context-engineering guidance favors over dumping everything into context. Anthropic's internal CLUE security tool demonstrates the scaled version: an orchestrator fans out parallel sub-agents to enrich a task with context from Slack, internal docs, code, and data warehouses, returning condensed summaries. The MCP server respects existing permissions via OAuth, and a strong caveat across sources is to keep a human review gate (markdown-first, verify quotes/snippets) before trusting or republishing AI-gathered context.

techniques.name: Search-then-fetch over Confluence (CQL) and Jira (JQL)
techniques.description: Don't ask Claude to read a whole space. First run a search to find candidates, then fetch only the relevant pages/issues in full. The Atlassian MCP servers expose this two-step surface directly: confluence_search (CQL) + confluence_get_page to pull content, and jira_search (JQL) + jira_get_issue. Practical prompt shape: 'Search Confluence for pages about <feature area>, list the top 5 with titles and links, then fetch the two most relevant and summarize the decisions.' This is the literal mechanic of mining the wiki.

techniques.name: Traverse Jira issue -> linked Confluence design doc
techniques.description: Start from the backlog item itself. Claude can pull a Jira issue, follow its links to the related Confluence design/RFC page, and summarize both in one response — exactly the onboarding-to-an-unfamiliar-area workflow practitioners cite. Lets you go from a vague ticket to the surrounding decision context (why, prior art, constraints) without manually chasing links.

techniques.name: Mine page comments and history for tribal knowledge
techniques.description: The decisions and caveats that don't make it into the page body often live in comments, inline comments, and edit history (who changed what, when). When mining for feature context, explicitly ask Claude to pull page comments and recent revisions, not just the rendered body — that's where 'we tried X and it broke' lives. (Anthropic frames timestamps/metadata as proxies for relevance during agentic exploration.)

techniques.name: Just-in-time retrieval with lightweight identifiers
techniques.description: Pass Claude page IDs, stored CQL/JQL queries, and links rather than pasting entire documents up front. Let the agent load full content only when it decides it needs it ('load what you need when you need it'). This avoids stuffing the context window with stale or irrelevant doc dumps and keeps retrieval focused — Anthropic contrasts this favorably with classic pre-loaded RAG and notes hybrid (a few docs up front + tools to fetch the rest) often wins.

techniques.name: Parallel sub-agents for multi-source enrichment (the CLUE pattern)
techniques.description: Anthropic's security team built CLUE (Claude Looks Up Evidence): an orchestrator issues commands to sub-agents that run queries in parallel across Slack, internal docs, code repos, and data warehouses, each returning a condensed 1-2k-token summary. For feature refinement, the analog is fanning out research across Confluence + Jira + the codebase simultaneously, each sub-agent reporting back a distilled finding rather than raw pages — keeping the main context clean. Cited scale: ~25 tool calls and ~11 queries per investigation, beyond manual capacity.

techniques.name: Structured note-taking / memory while researching
techniques.description: Have Claude write findings (key decisions, owners, open questions, doc links) to a persistent notes/memory file as it mines, rather than holding everything in the live context window. This survives compaction on long research sessions and becomes the seed for the feature spec — Anthropic cites this for tracking progress and dependencies across long-running tasks.

techniques.name: Guard against context rot from internal docs
techniques.description: Internal wikis are full of outdated, duplicate, and contradictory pages. Anthropic names four failure modes to watch: context poisoning (stale/wrong info), distraction (noise), confusion (similar-but-distinct pages mixed up), and clash (contradictory statements). When mining Confluence, curate aggressively — prefer recently-updated pages, ask Claude to flag conflicts between sources, and don't treat every retrieved page as ground truth.

techniques.name: OAuth + existing permissions as the access boundary
techniques.description: The official Atlassian Remote MCP server runs as a hosted (Cloudflare) service and 'respects all your existing permission controls' via OAuth — Claude only sees what the authenticated user can see, so mining doesn't create a new data-exfiltration path. Caveat to state plainly to a security-conscious audience: it's a remote service, so you're trusting Atlassian's infrastructure rather than running locally; community servers like sooperset/mcp-atlassian can run self-hosted against Server/Data Center if that matters.

techniques.name: Human review gate: markdown-first, verify before trusting
techniques.description: A consistent practitioner caveat: don't let AI-gathered or AI-generated context flow straight back into Confluence or into the spec unchecked. Generate a local markdown draft of the synthesized context first, verify code snippets and quoted decisions against the real source pages, then publish/commit. Prevents propagating hallucinated or stale 'facts' as if they were team knowledge.

notableQuotesOrExamples: Setup (Claude Code, official remote server): `claude mcp add atlassian --transport sse "https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/sse" --scope user`

Atlassian Remote MCP can 'Summarize Jira work items or Confluence pages' and 'Enrich Jira work items with context from many different sources that Claude has access to' — and 'respects all your existing permission controls' via OAuth.

CLUE (Claude Looks Up Evidence): 'an orchestrator issues commands to sub-agents that execute queries in parallel,' handling investigations of '25 tool calls and nearly 11 queries per session.' Jackie Bow: 'That internal context is the missing piece that really helps alerts be contextualized for your environment.'

Anthropic context-engineering: keep 'lightweight identifiers (file paths, stored queries, web links, etc.)' and let agents load detail at runtime; sub-agents 'return only a condensed, distilled summary of its work (often 1,000-2,000 tokens).'
Concrete read tools (sooperset/mcp-atlassian): confluence_search (CQL), confluence_get_page, jira_search (JQL), jira_get_issue — i.e. search then fetch.
Markdown-first caveat: 'Please create a comprehensive ... documentation as a Markdown file first. I want to review and improve the content before publishing it to Confluence.'

angle: Mining Slack / team chat history with AI to recover decisions and context relevant to a feature — squarely the Research phase of the refinement loop, with spillover into Plan and Share.
summary: A backlog feature's "why" is usually buried in old Slack threads — decisions, constraints, and abandoned approaches that never made it into a ticket. Practitioner and vendor sources converge on a workable pattern: connect Claude (Claude Code or the Claude app) to Slack via an MCP server or the official connector, then have it search history by date/user/keyword, read full threads, and synthesize scattered messages into a coherent decision record — catching implicit decisions like "yeah we should add rate limiting before launch" that keyword search misses. Slack's own engineering team built a RAG bot over message history plus docs and canvases that saved an estimated 3,000+ hours, but reports hallucinations and weak multi-step reasoning. The recurring caveat across sources: chat AI is retrieval infrastructure, not knowledge capture — summaries are ephemeral and stateless, so the engineer must durably write recovered context back into the ticket/spec or it's lost again.

techniques.name: Connect Slack to Claude over MCP and search by date/user/keyword
techniques.description: The official Slack MCP server exposes search tools that filter messages and files by date, user, and content type, plus tools to read full channel history and complete thread conversations. Set up via `claude mcp add` with OAuth. Scope it down for safety: read-only history mining needs scopes like channels:history, groups:history, and search:read; message posting is disabled by default in community servers. Watch the constraints — search has special rate limits, and only directory-published or internal Slack apps may use MCP.
techniques.whenToUse: Research — first pass to locate every thread that touched the feature area before writing anything.

techniques.name: Synthesize scattered messages into a decision record (catch implicit decisions)
techniques.description: Rather than listing messages verbatim, prompt Claude to group related messages and explain WHY each decision was made. A concrete three-prompt flow: (1) 'Summarize the Slack messages about X with context on why each was sent,' (2) 'From this summary, what do I need to follow up on and what does the team need to do?', (3) create tickets from the action items. The reported payoff is that Claude surfaces implicit, easily-lost decisions such as an offhand 'yeah we should add rate limiting before launch' that keyword search would never connect to the feature.
techniques.whenToUse: Research → Plan — turning raw thread output into the constraints and follow-ups that shape the spec and tickets.

techniques.name: Natural-language 'what did we decide' queries instead of keyword search
techniques.description: Ask conversational questions like 'What did we decide about the Q3 launch date?' — the system retrieves by meaning/intent rather than exact terms, described as the highest-value feature for knowledge-management use cases. This recovers decisions when you don't remember the exact wording used in the original thread. Hard limit: it only searches what is in Slack — Confluence, Drive, CRM, and email are out of reach, so pair it with other sources.
techniques.whenToUse: Research — recovering a specific past decision when you know the topic but not the keywords.

techniques.name: RAG over chat history + docs + canvases (Slack's own engineering bot)
techniques.description: Slack's internal engineering bot indexes three sources — channel-relevant technical docs, historical posts via the message search API, and Canvas docs via the canvas search API — vectorized in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. It runs in two modes: triggered by a specific emoji reaction (reacji), or actively monitoring an escalation channel and stepping in when it detects a topic it can help with, using an LLM to classify posts into categories (announcements, how-to, human-action-needed, PR reviews, service issues, unknown). Estimated 3,000+ engineering hours saved across 25+ channels. Caveat from the team itself: hallucinations and weak multi-step reasoning limited its use on complex technical problems, and tuning third-party knowledge integration was intensive.
techniques.whenToUse: Research — for teams that want a persistent, queryable layer over chat history rather than ad-hoc per-feature searches.

techniques.name: Tag Claude in the thread to pull context where the decision happened
techniques.description: With the Claude Code in Slack integration (research preview, launched Dec 8 2025), mentioning @Claude in a channel or thread has it assess whether the task is a coding task, gather recent messages — including stack traces, log fragments, and error screenshots converted to text plus earlier discussion — and use that to determine the relevant linked repository, then post progress and a pull request back into the thread. For feature refinement the valuable part is the context-gathering: Claude reading the live discussion in place rather than you exporting it. Caveats: repo disambiguation logic is unspecified, and it adds dependencies (Slack/Claude outages or rate limits can disrupt the workflow), plus code-security/IP considerations.
techniques.whenToUse: Research → Build/Share — grabbing context at the point of discussion and looping work back to the people who had it.

techniques.name: Durably persist recovered context — chat AI is retrieval, not capture
techniques.description: The cross-cutting caveat: Slack AI is stateless and ephemeral — 'Each conversation starts fresh. There is no memory of previous interactions... no accumulated context over time,' and it's retrieval infrastructure rather than knowledge-capture infrastructure. Practically this means a Claude-generated thread summary vanishes unless you write it somewhere durable. The actionable move for refinement: immediately fold recovered decisions/constraints into the Jira/Linear ticket or spec doc (the Slack-to-Linear workflow does exactly this by creating tickets from the synthesis), so the next person doesn't have to re-mine the same history.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan → Share — converting transient recovered context into a permanent artifact attached to the feature.

notableQuotesOrExamples: Implicit decision recovery: Claude catches throwaway lines like 'yeah we should add rate limiting before launch' that keyword search would miss (samuellawrentz).
Three-prompt mining flow: 'Summarize the Slack messages about X with context on why each was sent' → 'what do I need to follow up on?' → create tickets (samuellawrentz).
Natural-language decision query: 'What did we decide about the Q3 launch date?' retrieves by meaning, not exact terms (questionbase).
Slack's bot triggers two ways: a specific emoji reaction (reacji) or by monitoring an escalation channel and jumping in when it detects a topic it can help with (slack.engineering).
Stateless caveat: 'Each conversation starts fresh. There is no memory of previous interactions, no learning from how your team works, no accumulated context over time' (questionbase).
Example search prompt: 'Search my Slack workspace for messages about the product launch and summarize the key decisions' (awesomeclaude).

angle: Real-world engineering-team case studies and retrospectives on adopting Claude Code for feature work — what concrete workflows practitioners actually run, mapped to the Pick→Research→Plan→Build→Verify→Share loop, with the skeptical caveats they learned the hard way.
summary: Across a staff engineer's 6-week retrospective (Sanity), an engineering-team onboarding writeup (incident.io), a tech-debt case study (Faros), and Anthropic's own internal usage research, the consistent pattern is that Claude Code works best as a fast, fallible junior engineer: you scope small, well-defined, easily-verifiable work; feed it persistent context (CLAUDE.md, MCP to Linear/GitHub/docs); expect the first attempt to be largely wrong and iterate; and gate everything behind objective verification (build + tests) plus human review. Anthropic's data quantifies the shift — feature-implementation work rose from 14.3% to 36.9% of Claude Code usage (Feb–Aug 2025) and engineers saw a 67% increase in merged PRs/day — while the role shifts toward reviewing rather than writing net-new code. The sharpest disagreement is over the Plan phase: Anthropic keeps high-level design human-reserved (design/planning only grew 1%→9.9%), whereas Sanity and incident.io actively push Claude into drafting specs and plans. Practitioners are unanimous that "it works" is insufficient validation — Claude overengineers, invents out-of-scope features, and claims fuller codebase analysis than it performed.

techniques.name: Scope to small, verifiable, low-risk slices
techniques.description: Deliberately pick features/tasks that are small, well-defined, self-contained (decoupled from larger systems), and objectively verifiable. Faros chose a tech-debt task precisely because it had low business-logic risk, was verifiable via build+tests, and was high manual effort (200+ files of duplicated helpers). Anthropic engineers report they delegate most readily when work is 'easily verifiable' and 'self-contained.'

techniques.name: Read the relevant CLAUDE.md files first to orient
techniques.description: Treat per-area CLAUDE.md files as both AI context and human onboarding docs: they explain the architectural approach, point to resources, and give usage examples. The incident.io engineer's first step in an unfamiliar part of the codebase is to read the relevant CLAUDE.md files to orient. These files must be revised over time — a known anti-pattern is writing them once and never updating them.

techniques.name: Wire up MCP to your real systems (read-only) to skip re-explaining context
techniques.description: Connect Claude to Linear/Jira, Notion, GitHub, databases (read-only), and the codebase via MCP so it starts with project context instead of you repeating constraints every session. Sanity: 'Without this context, you're explaining the same constraints repeatedly. With it, you start at attempt two instead of attempt one.' incident.io 'rubber ducks' by having Claude search prior Linear tickets to surface past debugging discussions.

techniques.name: Ask Claude to diagram the existing flow before changing it
techniques.description: For complex event-driven or multi-step systems, have Claude visualize the flow (e.g. HTTP endpoint → Pub/Sub → handlers → cascading events) to build a shared mental model before planning a change. incident.io did this for their call-transcription service; note it took iteration — they used a custom sub-agent to 'boilerplate a good diagramming prompt.'

techniques.name: Split large work into multiple sequential PRs up front
techniques.description: Rather than one giant change, decompose into reviewable, independently-verifiable PRs. Faros split a 200-file refactor into PR 1 (source utilities, 105 files) and PR 2 (destination utilities, ~95 files). Decomposition also mitigates Claude's context-window limits on large codebases (a failure mode Sanity calls out explicitly).

techniques.name: The three-attempt framework (expect attempt 1 to be ~95% garbage)
techniques.description: Sanity's staff engineer treats the first attempt as context-building, not delivery: attempt 1 is mostly wrong but reveals the real challenges, attempt 2 understands nuances but often still unusable, attempt 3 yields a workable iteration starting point. Reframes early bad output as part of the process rather than failure — and argues for deliberately giving one feature several attempts rather than abandoning after the first.

techniques.name: Capture discoveries mid-task and fold them back into context
techniques.description: Use a slash command (incident.io's /note_this) to summarize discoveries during a task and append to feature-specific notes, then later convert those notes into CLAUDE.md entries for future developers. Combats Claude's lack of memory across sessions and prevents it repeating the same mistakes (the 'learning problem' Sanity describes).

techniques.name: Make build + tests the objective gate, not 'it works'
techniques.description: Define success criteria that are automatable. Faros: 'if the project built and tests passed, we were good,' relying on standard CI rather than manual review for a mechanical refactor. But practitioners warn 'it works as intended' is insufficient validation on its own — kleiber.me mandates a real code review on top, with the directive to 'solve the underlying issue and don't create a hacky solution.'

techniques.name: Layered review: Claude self-review, then human, then team
techniques.description: Sanity runs a three-tier review: Claude self-reviews for test coverage/bugs/improvements; the engineer reviews for maintainability, architecture, business logic, and integration points; then normal team review (where most reviewers don't notice the code was AI-generated). The engineer argues reviewing without ego ('No emotional attachment means better reviews') makes it easier to delete bad solutions.

techniques.name: Guard against scope creep and partial analysis explicitly
techniques.description: Claude invents out-of-scope features (kleiber: when asked to streamline docs it added a Discord group, support email, and 'best practices' unprompted) and selectively examines files while claiming a comprehensive review, leaving refactors half-done. Mitigate with a written spec file to constrain scope, linters/git hooks/tests as guardrails, and a review that checks whether the whole change was actually made.

techniques.name: Track parallel AI work in your tracker and mark human edits
techniques.description: When running multiple threads, track everything in the issue tracker (Linear) to avoid confusion across instances, explicitly mark human-edited code so Claude knows what changed, and never parallelize identical problem spaces. incident.io's /copy slash command pipes Claude output to the clipboard for use elsewhere (e.g. Grafana queries).

techniques.name: Expect the role to shift from author to reviewer
techniques.description: Anthropic's internal data shows the human turn becoming editorial: one engineer reported '70%+ [shifted] to being a code reviewer/reviser rather than a net-new code writer,' average task complexity rose 3.2→3.8/5, Claude chained 21.2 consecutive tool calls (up 116%), and merged PRs/engineer/day rose 67%. Yet over half of engineers say they can 'fully delegate' only 0–20% of work — supervision stays mandatory.

notableQuotesOrExamples: Sanity: 'Pick one small, well-defined feature. Give AI three attempts at implementing it.' — attempt 1 ~95% garbage (context-building), attempt 2 ~50% garbage, attempt 3 workable.
Sanity: 'This isn't failure; it's the process!' and 'I don't care about "my code" anymore; it's just output to review and refine.' Reports shipping features 2–3x faster at a ~$1000–1500/month cost.

Anthropic: feature-implementation work rose 14.3%→36.9% of Claude Code usage (Feb–Aug 2025); 67% increase in merged PRs per engineer per day; one engineer: '70%+ [changed] to being a code reviewer/reviser rather than a net-new code writer.'

Anthropic (the Plan-phase caveat): design/planning grew only 1%→9.9% because engineers keep 'high-level thinking and design decisions' that require organizational context and judgment — over half can 'fully delegate' only 0–20% of work.

Faros: a 200+ file tech-debt refactor split into two PRs (105 + ~95 files), gated purely on 'if the project built and tests passed, we were good,' which then unlocked a Docker multi-stage build cutting the image from 752MB to 376MB.

incident.io: 'Whenever I start a task in a part of the codebase I'm unfamiliar with, my first step is to go through the relevant CLAUDE.md files to help orientate myself' — and the engineer 'shipped value by day two.' Caveat: Claude 'often writes invalid' Claude settings files.

kleiber.me (skeptic): asked to streamline docs, Claude unprompted added a Discord group, support email, and developer best practices; it also refactors only partial implementations 'while claiming comprehensive project review.'

angle: Hooks, automation, and guardrails in Claude Code that improve feature-development quality — mapped across the Pick → Research → Plan → Build → Verify → Share refinement loop.
summary: Claude Code's quality story rests on a layered governance loop: CLAUDE.md sets advisory standards, hooks enforce them deterministically (they are shell commands, not prompts, so the model can't forget), and CI re-validates at merge. The official docs document the key practitioner-visible events (PreToolUse and UserPromptSubmit can block; PostToolUse, Notification, SessionStart, Stop run on lifecycle points) configured as a hooks object in settings.json, where a hook exiting with code 2 blocks the action and feeds stderr back to Claude. Beyond hooks, Anthropic emphasizes giving Claude a verifiable check it can run (tests, build exit code, screenshot diff) so the agent closes its own loop, separating explore/plan from implementation via plan mode, and adding a fresh-context adversarial reviewer (the bundled /code-review subagent) before counting work done. A notable skeptical finding: several popular hook tutorials ship configs that will not actually load because they use YAML or a `handler` key instead of the documented `hooks: [{type, command}]` array.

techniques.name: CLAUDE.md as enforced-then-pruned standards layer
techniques.description: CLAUDE.md is read at the start of every session and is the right place for non-obvious build/test commands, code style that differs from defaults, and repo etiquette. It is advisory only. Anthropic's explicit failure mode: an over-long CLAUDE.md causes Claude to ignore half of it because rules get lost in noise — for each line ask 'would removing this cause a mistake?' and if a rule keeps being violated, convert it to a hook rather than adding emphasis.
techniques.whenToUse: Pick / Research — establishes persistent project context before any work; revisited continuously

techniques.name: Explore-then-plan-then-code with plan mode and interview-to-SPEC.md
techniques.description: Separate research and planning from implementation to avoid solving the wrong problem. Use plan mode (Claude reads files, answers questions, makes no changes), open the plan in your editor with Ctrl+G to edit before execution, then switch out to implement. For larger features, start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to interview you using the AskUserQuestion tool until everything is covered, then write a self-contained SPEC.md (names files/interfaces, states what is out of scope, ends with an end-to-end verification step) and execute it in a fresh session.
techniques.whenToUse: Research / Plan — scoping the vague backlog idea into a precise, verifiable spec

techniques.name: SessionStart context injection
techniques.description: A SessionStart hook can return additionalContext that is injected at session start (e.g. current branch, pending issues, environment notes) so every run begins with the same baseline context rather than relying on the user to re-state it. Deterministic, runs every session, cannot block.
techniques.whenToUse: Pick / Research — automatically seeds context at the start of each refinement session

techniques.name: Subagent investigation to protect main context
techniques.description: Delegate codebase research to a subagent ('use subagents to investigate how X works and whether reusable utilities exist'). The subagent reads many files in its own context window and reports back only a summary, keeping the main conversation clean for implementation — directly mitigating the documented 'infinite exploration' failure where unscoped investigation fills context and degrades performance.
techniques.whenToUse: Research — exploring an unfamiliar area without polluting the working session

techniques.name: PostToolUse auto-format on every edit
techniques.description: A PostToolUse hook with an Edit|Write matcher runs deterministically after any file-editing tool. The documented pattern extracts the edited path with jq and pipes it to a formatter, so formatting stays consistent without the model choosing to do it. Lowest-risk, highest-frequency first hook to add. Note PostToolUse fires after the action and cannot undo it — it is for formatting/logging/validation, not prevention.
techniques.whenToUse: Build — keeps generated code consistent as it is written

techniques.name: PreToolUse blocking guardrails (protected files, dangerous commands)
techniques.description: A PreToolUse hook can block a tool call before it runs by exiting with code 2 (stderr is fed back to Claude so it can adjust) or by returning a permissionDecision of 'deny'. The official example checks the target path against a protected-pattern list (.env, package-lock.json, .git/) and blocks the edit; the same shape blocks destructive Bash like rm -rf. Practitioners extend this to block force-push and unreviewed dependency installs (supply-chain protection). Caveat: regex/pattern guards let novel destructive patterns slip through, so pair with git history and sandboxing rather than treating hooks as sole defense; over-blocking frustrates workflows, so document exceptions.
techniques.whenToUse: Build — prevents the agent from touching sensitive paths or running destructive commands

techniques.name: Prompt/agent hooks for judgment-based guardrails
techniques.description: When a rule needs judgment rather than a deterministic pattern, hooks can be type 'prompt' or type 'agent', using a Claude model to evaluate the condition (e.g. semantically classify whether an edit touches auth, payments, or secrets and deny if so). This catches context that static regex misses. Practitioner caveat: add prompt-based hooks only after command hooks are stable, since they add latency and a model call on every matched event.
techniques.whenToUse: Build — semantic guardrails on sensitive edits where regex is too brittle

techniques.name: Give Claude a verifiable check so the loop closes itself
techniques.description: Without a check it can run, 'looks done' is the only signal and the human becomes the verification loop. Provide something returning pass/fail — a test suite, build exit code, linter, fixture diff, or screenshot compared to a design — and ask Claude to run it and iterate in the same prompt. Have it show evidence (test output, the command and its result) rather than asserting success.
techniques.whenToUse: Verify — turns an unattended session into one that self-corrects to a passing check

techniques.name: Stop hook as a deterministic completion gate
techniques.description: A Stop hook runs your check (tests/build) as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes — the hardest gate, useful for unattended runs. Important documented limit: Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks, so a Stop gate cannot trap the agent forever and is not a substitute for a check that can actually be satisfied.
techniques.whenToUse: Verify — enforces that a turn cannot end with a failing check

techniques.name: Adversarial fresh-context review before done
techniques.description: Before counting work complete, have a reviewer run in a fresh subagent context that sees only the diff and the criteria, not the reasoning that produced it. The bundled /code-review skill reviews the current diff for bugs and returns findings into the session; to check against the plan, write your own prompt naming the work, the plan (e.g. PLAN.md), and what counts as a finding. Documented caveat: a reviewer asked to find gaps will report some even when the work is sound, leading to over-engineering — instruct it to flag only correctness/requirement gaps and treat the rest as optional.
techniques.whenToUse: Verify / Share — independent quality check before opening a PR

techniques.name: Headless mode and the governance loop into CI
techniques.description: claude -p 'prompt' runs non-interactively for CI pipelines, pre-commit hooks, and fan-out scripts, with --output-format json/stream-json for parsing and --allowedTools to scope permissions for unattended runs. The recommended end-to-end pattern is a three-layer governance loop: CLAUDE.md defines standards, hooks enforce them locally and non-bypassably, and the same gates (lint, type-check, security) re-run in CI so AI-generated code meets the same bar as human code before merge.
techniques.whenToUse: Share — gating the change in CI and scripting batch/migration work

techniques.name: Permission allowlists, auto mode, and sandboxing to reduce rubber-stamping
techniques.description: After the tenth approval you are clicking, not reviewing. Reduce interruptions three ways: /permissions allowlists for known-safe commands (npm run lint, git commit), auto mode where a separate classifier model blocks risky actions (scope escalation, unknown infrastructure) while letting routine work proceed, and /sandbox for OS-level filesystem/network isolation. In headless auto-mode runs the classifier aborts if it repeatedly blocks, since there is no human fallback.
techniques.whenToUse: Build — keeps the human as a meaningful approver instead of a rubber stamp

notableQuotesOrExamples: Official auto-format hook (verbatim from docs, .claude/settings.json): {"hooks":{"PostToolUse":[{"matcher":"Edit|Write","hooks":[{"type":"command","command":"jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npx prettier --write"}]}]}}

Official protected-files guard (verbatim, .claude/hooks/protect-files.sh): reads stdin, FILE_PATH=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // empty'); PROTECTED_PATTERNS=(".env" "package-lock.json" ".git/"); on match it echoes 'Blocked: ... matches protected pattern' to stderr and runs exit 2 to block the edit.

Exit-code contract (docs): 0 = success and stdout/JSON is parsed; 2 = blocking error (blocks the PreToolUse action / rejects the UserPromptSubmit) with stderr fed back to Claude; any other code = non-blocking error, execution continues.
Fan-out batch pattern (docs): for file in $(cat files.txt); do claude -p "Migrate $file ... Return OK or FAIL." --allowedTools "Edit,Bash(git commit *)"; done
Caveat from docs paraphrase: a Stop hook blocks the turn from ending until the check passes, but Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks.

Skeptical finding (cross-source): popular hook tutorials ship configs that will not load — paddo.dev uses a YAML event/pattern/action format and pixelmojo uses a 'handler' key, whereas the documented schema is a hooks object with per-event arrays of {matcher, hooks:[{type,command}]}.

angle: MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers connecting Claude to JIRA, Confluence, GitHub, and Slack as context sources across the feature-refinement loop
summary: MCP is Anthropic's open standard for two-way connections between AI tools and data sources, replacing per-source custom integrations; Anthropic ships reference servers for GitHub, Slack, Git, Postgres, and others, and a growing set of vendors host remote servers Claude connects to via the MCP connector API. For feature refinement the highest-value pattern is letting Claude "walk Jira, GitHub, and Confluence in one pass" — pulling a backlog ticket, its linked runbooks, related issues, and code into a single context window, then writing back (creating issues, updating status, posting summaries). Practitioners are blunt about limits: read operations are reliable but cross-tool write workflows hit rate limits and auth friction, native integrations often beat MCP for production automation, and a short tool list (5-6 servers) matters because the model weighs every tool on every turn. Source recency also bites — the GitHub npm server is deprecated (use the remote HTTP server) and Slack is OAuth remote-only, so older setup guides ship stale commands.

techniques.name: Pick the next ticket from the Jira backlog via the Atlassian MCP
techniques.description: Connect Claude to the official Atlassian Remote MCP server (OAuth, hosted by Atlassian, respects your existing Jira/Confluence permissions). Ask Claude to search and summarize open backlog issues so you can surface and rank candidates without leaving the editor. Read operations (searching, viewing) are the reliable sweet spot per practitioners.
techniques.whenToUse: Pick — selecting which backlog feature to refine next

techniques.name: Walk Jira + Confluence + GitHub in one pass for context
techniques.description: The headline payoff: with multiple MCP servers connected, Claude pulls a Jira ticket, its linked Confluence runbooks/specs, related Jira issues, and relevant GitHub code into a single context window — eliminating context-switching and producing a richer understanding of the feature before any code is written. Atlassian's own incident example: query service ownership, pull recent issues, search Confluence runbooks, and surface it all in one summary.
techniques.whenToUse: Research — gathering all existing context on a vague feature idea

techniques.name: Batch-create issues and sharpen acceptance criteria with write-back
techniques.description: The Atlassian MCP can create Jira issues and Confluence pages directly from Claude, including batch creation of several related issues at once, and can enrich existing work items with context from other connected sources. Use this to break a refined feature into subtasks and cross-reference Confluence docs to tighten acceptance criteria. Caveat: write/automation workflows are less reliable than reads.
techniques.whenToUse: Plan — decomposing the feature into tickets and acceptance criteria

techniques.name: Connect the GitHub MCP server for issue/PR/code context (use the remote HTTP server)
techniques.description: The GitHub MCP server gives Claude tools for issues, pull requests, code search, and Actions. Connect via the remote Streamable-HTTP endpoint with a fine-grained PAT: `claude mcp add-json github '{"type":"http","url":"https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp","headers":{"Authorization":"Bearer YOUR_GITHUB_PAT"}}'`. IMPORTANT conflict: the official GitHub docs mark the npm package `@modelcontextprotocol/server-github` deprecated as of April 2025, yet many third-party guides still hand it out — prefer the remote HTTP server or the Docker local server.
techniques.whenToUse: Build — bringing repo code, issues, and PR context to Claude while implementing

techniques.name: Use the GitHub MCP Actions tools to check CI on the work
techniques.description: The GitHub MCP server exposes Actions/workflow tools, letting Claude trigger and inspect workflow runs against the branch. This is a thinner part of the MCP story — practitioners report cross-tool and real-time-sync workflows are unreliable and recommend native CI integrations (GitHub Actions, Jenkins) for anything critical — so treat MCP here as a read/inspect aid, not the automation backbone.
techniques.whenToUse: Verify — checking that CI/workflows pass on the implemented feature

techniques.name: Close the loop: update Jira status, write the Confluence page, post a Slack summary
techniques.description: Use the Atlassian MCP to transition the Jira issue and publish/update a Confluence page documenting the shipped work, then the Slack MCP server to post a summary to the team channel. Slack's MCP server is remote/hosted-only (`https://mcp.slack.com/mcp`) via OAuth — install in Claude Code with `claude plugin install slack`; older guides that show an `npx @modelcontextprotocol/server-slack` local command are stale.
techniques.whenToUse: Share — communicating shipped work and updating tracking/docs

techniques.name: Scope servers and apply least privilege deliberately
techniques.description: Put stable servers (GitHub, Slack, filesystem) at user scope (~/.claude/settings.json) and project-specific ones (databases, monitoring) at project scope (.claude/settings.json), which overrides user scope. Use fine-grained tokens with minimal scopes, prefer read-only DB roles, keep settings files out of version control, and run each server manually once to complete first-time OAuth before wiring it in. Treat every MCP server like a CLI tool acting with your account's permissions.

techniques.name: Keep the tool list short to protect context and accuracy
techniques.description: The model has to consider every connected tool on every turn, so a short tool list matters more than people expect — practitioners recommend ~5-6 servers maximum and pruning the long tail. Use tool name/filter fields to resolve collisions when two servers expose similarly named tools.
techniques.whenToUse: Cross-cutting — governs how many servers to enable for any refinement session

notableQuotesOrExamples: Anthropic's MCP announcement: MCP is "an open standard that enables developers to build secure, two-way connections between their data sources and AI-powered tools," with reference servers for Google Drive, Slack, GitHub, Git, Postgres, and Puppeteer.

"The payoff shows up when Claude can walk Jira, GitHub, and Confluence in one pass" — and Atlassian's incident example: query Compass for service ownership, pull recent Jira issues, search Confluence runbooks, and surface it all in a single summary.
Atlassian Remote MCP "features OAuth authentication and respects all your existing permission controls" — users cannot exceed their normal Jira/Confluence permissions through Claude.

Skeptic's reality check: "native tool integrations often outperform MCP solutions" for production; "simple read operations (searching, viewing) work consistently" while complex cross-tool workflows fail on rate limits/auth; realistic setup is "weeks to months, not hours."
On context cost: "A short tool list matters more than people expect. The model has to consider every tool on every turn" — recommend five or six servers maximum.

Source-staleness conflict: GitHub's official docs say "The npm package @modelcontextprotocol/server-github is deprecated as of April 2025" (use the remote HTTP server), yet third-party guides still recommend it; similarly Slack's server is remote/hosted-only despite guides showing a local npx command.

angle: AI-assisted code review and PR workflows as part of refining and shipping a feature (Verify -> Share phases of the loop, with hooks back into Build).
summary: Anthropic's own docs and tooling treat AI review as a separate, fresh-context step that grades work the implementing session didn't produce: a "Writer/Reviewer" two-session pattern, an adversarial review subagent (and the bundled /code-review skill) that sees only the diff plus criteria, and dedicated security review via the /security-review command and the claude-code-security-review GitHub Action (diff-aware, posts inline PR comments, filters low-impact false positives). Practitioners converge on a division of labor where the AI handles the mechanical first pass (security, style/arch conformance, test adequacy) while humans keep acceptance and strategy decisions; rollout is best phased (shadow mode, then block only critical findings). The strongest caveats come from Anthropic itself: a reviewer prompted to find gaps will invent some, leading to over-engineering, and the security action is "not hardened against prompt injection" so it should only review trusted PRs.

techniques.name: Writer/Reviewer two-session pattern
techniques.description: Run one Claude session to implement, then a SECOND, fresh session to review that code (e.g. 'Review the rate limiter in @src/middleware/rateLimiter.ts. Look for edge cases, race conditions, and consistency with existing middleware'), and feed its output back to the writer session to address. Fresh context matters: 'a fresh context improves code review since Claude won't be biased toward code it just wrote.'
techniques.whenToUse: Verify (with a loop back into Build to fix findings)

techniques.name: Adversarial review subagent on the diff
techniques.description: Before calling work done, have a subagent review the diff in a fresh context against the plan: 'Use a subagent to review the rate limiter diff against PLAN.md. Check that every requirement is implemented, the listed edge cases have tests, and nothing outside the task's scope changed. Report gaps, not style preferences.' The subagent sees only the diff and criteria, not the reasoning that produced it, so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it. Findings return directly to the implementing session for fix-and-re-review.

techniques.name: Bundled /code-review skill
techniques.description: Run the bundled /code-review slash command to review the current diff for bugs in a fresh subagent and return findings to the session, without writing your own reviewer prompt.

techniques.name: Define a reusable security-reviewer subagent
techniques.description: Add a .claude/agents/security-reviewer.md with a role ('senior security engineer') and a scoped checklist (injection, authn/authz flaws, secrets in code, insecure data handling) plus restricted tools (Read, Grep, Glob, Bash). Then invoke explicitly: 'Use a subagent to review this code for security issues.'

techniques.name: /security-review command and the security-review GitHub Action
techniques.description: Use the /security-review command in the terminal before committing, or wire up the claude-code-security-review Action to run on PR open. It is diff-aware ('only analyzes changed files'), follows PR analysis -> contextual review -> findings with severity -> false-positive filtering -> inline PR comments, and detects injection, broken authn/authz, hardcoded secrets, weak crypto, insecure deserialization/RCE, and XSS. It auto-excludes low-impact/false-positive-prone classes (DoS, rate limiting, generic input validation without proven impact, open redirects); customize via a false-positive-filtering-instructions file or by copying security-review.md into .claude/commands/.

techniques.name: Headless Claude in CI / PR pipelines
techniques.description: Use non-interactive mode (claude -p "prompt") with --output-format json or stream-json to run review/lint/test checks in CI pipelines, pre-commit hooks, or scripts; scope what it can do with --allowedTools when running unattended.

techniques.name: gh CLI for the PR step
techniques.description: Install the gh CLI so Claude can create issues, open pull requests, and read PR comments context-efficiently (without it, unauthenticated GitHub API calls hit rate limits). A typical close-out prompt: 'commit with a descriptive message and open a PR.'

techniques.name: CLAUDE.md as the review standards file
techniques.description: Check a concise CLAUDE.md into git holding repository etiquette (branch naming, PR conventions), code-style rules that differ from defaults, testing instructions, and architectural decisions — the persistent standards an AI reviewer checks against. Keep it short: bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore rules. Prune anything Claude already does correctly or convert it to a hook.

techniques.name: AI first-pass, human acceptance split (with phased rollout)
techniques.description: Let the AI agent handle the mechanical first pass — security scanning, style/architecture conformance, test adequacy, spec checks — while humans review acceptance and strategy: does this PR solve the right problem, fit the architecture, respect UX and long-term cost. Assign the agent an explicit role ('Staff Security Engineer', 'Senior Code Reviewer'). Roll out in phases: shadow mode (no merge blocking) first, then block only on critical security findings, then expand — and still require one human acceptance review.

notableQuotesOrExamples: Anthropic docs on bias: 'a fresh context improves code review since Claude won't be biased toward code it just wrote.'

Skeptic's caveat from Anthropic docs: 'A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound... Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering: extra abstraction layers, defensive code, and tests for cases that can't happen.'
Reviewer subagent prompt: 'Use a subagent to review the rate limiter diff against PLAN.md... Report gaps, not style preferences.'

Security action caveat: 'This action is not hardened against prompt injection attacks and should only be used to review trusted PRs.' (Anthropic recommends 'Require approval for all external contributors'.)
Division of labor (Medium): AI handles 'blocking & tackling' (security, style/arch conformance, test adequacy, spec checks); humans review 'acceptance & strategy.'
run-every-commit warning: it 'may increase false positives on PRs with many commits.'

angle: Community discussion and opinion (primarily Hacker News; Reddit was not directly retrievable) on how devs actually refine features with Claude, contrasted with Anthropic's official best-practices guidance.
summary: Across HN threads and Anthropic's own best-practices doc, the consensus refinement loop is: explore/research in read-only plan mode, force a written plan or spec before any code, implement against it, and gate "done" on a check Claude can run (tests, build, screenshot, or an adversarial review subagent). The official doc frames this as "explore, plan, code, commit" plus aggressive context hygiene (/clear between tasks, subagents for investigation) and a CLAUDE.md that compounds in value. But the community is openly skeptical that heavy spec/plan ceremony pays off: HN commenters argue a detailed-enough spec "is just code you can't run," demand measured evidence that spec-driven workflows beat plain plan mode, and warn that letting agents run unsupervised amplifies errors — favoring structured reusable skills over agents that "improvise on every task." Reddit r/ClaudeAI and r/ExperiencedDevs threads could not be fetched directly, so findings here are HN- and docs-weighted.

techniques.name: Explore, plan, code, commit (separate research from implementation)
techniques.description: Enter read-only plan mode first so Claude reads files and proposes an approach without editing; ask for a detailed implementation plan; only then switch out of plan mode to implement; finish by committing with a descriptive message and opening a PR. The doc cautions this adds overhead and to skip it for small, one-sentence-diff changes.

techniques.name: Let Claude interview you, then write a self-contained SPEC.md
techniques.description: Start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to interview you (via AskUserQuestion) about implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, and tradeoffs, then write a complete spec. The most useful specs name the files/interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step. Start a fresh session to execute the spec so context is clean.

techniques.name: Give Claude a check it can run (close the verification loop)
techniques.description: Provide a pass/fail signal Claude can read: example test cases in the prompt, a build, a linter, or a screenshot compared against a design. Have Claude show evidence (test output, command results, screenshots) rather than asserting success. Escalate gating from in-prompt, to a /goal condition re-checked each turn, to a Stop hook, to a second-opinion subagent.

techniques.name: Adversarial review in a fresh context
techniques.description: Before counting work as done, have a subagent (or the bundled /code-review) review the diff against the plan in a fresh context, seeing only the diff and criteria — not the reasoning that produced it. Tell the reviewer to flag only gaps affecting correctness or stated requirements, because a reviewer asked to find gaps will report some even when the work is sound, leading to over-engineering.

techniques.name: Manage context aggressively (/clear, subagents, CLAUDE.md)
techniques.description: Performance degrades as context fills, so /clear between unrelated tasks; after two failed corrections, clear and rewrite a better prompt rather than piling on. Delegate file-heavy investigation to subagents that report summaries without polluting the main conversation. Keep CLAUDE.md short — for each line ask 'would removing this cause a mistake?'; bloated files cause Claude to ignore actual instructions.

techniques.name: Two-dimensional spec decomposition with cleared context per step
techniques.description: Spec-driven advocate (HN post author sermakarevich) generates specs in steps — requirements, code analysis, design, implement — split into subtasks done sequentially, clearing context between steps to keep focus and reduce cost. Claimed to work especially well for platform-like apps with standardized plugins.

techniques.name: Reusable tested skills over per-task improvisation
techniques.description: An HN commenter (latand6) reports that 'a lot of the exhaustion comes from agents that improvise on every task' and that writing reusable skills so 'the agent follows a tested process instead of guessing' reduces wrong-half-the-time output and reviewer fatigue. Mirrors the doc's advice to encode repeatable workflows as skills.

techniques.name: Keep a human in the loop; don't run fully autonomous on costly feedback loops
techniques.description: A skeptical-but-positive HN commenter (bayareapsycho) keeps Claude inside the normal edit/debug loop rather than running many autonomous agents, reasoning that when 'claude alone vs claude+me is less accurate, that gets amplified' — especially when compile/test cycles are long. A counter-position in the same discussion runs many parallel agents; the two disagree.

notableQuotesOrExamples: HN commenter dwb on spec-driven workflows: 'A detailed-enough spec is just code that you can't run. If models and agents got to a point where doing a good job in Claude Code plan mode meant that I didn't have to keep an eye on them in implementation, then I would be interested in some bigger spec-driven thing like this.' (paraphrased-but-confirmed verbatim across two fetches)
HN commenter siliconc0w: 'Still not completely sold - it feels a bit like using power tools to shape wood but the final product needs a lot of sanding and polishing.'

HN commenter zihotki demanding evidence: 'How do you measure it actually works and you don't waste tokens and your personal time? I fail to see any backing for claims boosting performance and keeping costs low.'
HN commenter latand6: 'A lot of the exhaustion comes from agents that improvise on every task... The agent follows a tested process instead of guessing.'
HN commenter bayareapsycho on autonomy: 'if claude alone vs claude+me is less accurate, that gets amplified... Another reason why I don't like to let it run all by itself.'
Anthropic best-practices doc, the trust-then-verify failure pattern: 'Always provide verification (tests, scripts, screenshots). If you can't verify it, don't ship it.'
Anthropic doc on CLAUDE.md discipline: for each line ask 'Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes? If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions.'

angle: Pitfalls, failure modes, and anti-patterns when using Claude for feature work (confident-but-wrong, over-large diffs, lost context).
summary: Anthropic's own docs and practitioner write-ups converge on one root cause behind most Claude failures: the context window fills fast and quality degrades as it fills, so the operator stops being able to verify. The recurring failure modes are confident-but-wrong code (plausible output mistaken for correctness), context pollution (kitchen-sink sessions, repeated failed corrections, unscoped "investigate" reads), and unreviewable diffs. The fixes are structural rather than prompt-magic: scope tightly, separate explore/plan from build, give Claude a verifiable check it can run, clear context aggressively, and add a fresh-context adversarial review before calling work done. Note one genuine conflict in the sources: while practitioners push small single-purpose diffs, Anthropic warns that a hard "single-file changes only" rule can be an outdated constraint that blocks capable newer models from making coordinated cross-file edits.

techniques.name: Treat confidence as a guess, not evidence (trust-then-verify gap)
techniques.description: Claude produces plausible-looking implementations that miss edge cases and asserts success with phrases like 'should work', 'looks good', 'probably fine'. Anthropic's docs name this the 'trust-then-verify gap' and prescribe: always provide verification, and if you can't verify it, don't ship it. One practitioner reports shipping broken code three times in one week because the AI said 'should work' — the fix is to block confidence phrases and demand concrete evidence (test pass counts, build exit code, bundle size) instead.

techniques.name: Give Claude a check it can run (close the verification loop)
techniques.description: Without a runnable check, 'looks done' is the only stop signal and you become the verification loop, so every mistake waits for you to notice. Provide a test suite, build exit code, linter, fixture diff, or screenshot comparison so Claude runs the check, reads the result, and iterates until it passes. Phrase prompts with concrete acceptance criteria ('write validateEmail; user@.com is false; run the tests after implementing') and have Claude show the evidence (command output, screenshot) rather than asserting success. Escalation ladder: in-prompt check -> /goal condition re-checked every turn -> Stop hook that blocks the turn until the check passes.

techniques.name: Explore -> Plan -> then code (don't jump straight to implementation)
techniques.description: Letting Claude code immediately produces code that confidently solves the wrong problem. Use plan mode to read files and answer questions without edits, then ask for a detailed plan (files to change, flow, scope) before switching out of plan mode to implement against that plan. Caveat from the docs: planning adds overhead — if you could describe the diff in one sentence (typo, log line, rename), skip it. Planning pays off most when the approach is uncertain, the change spans multiple files, or you're unfamiliar with the code.

techniques.name: Have Claude interview you, then start a fresh session to execute the spec
techniques.description: For larger features, start with a minimal prompt and tell Claude to interview you using the AskUserQuestion tool about implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, and tradeoffs, then write a self-contained SPEC.md that names the files/interfaces involved, states what's out of scope, and ends with an end-to-end verification step. Then start a fresh session to execute it so implementation runs on clean context. Time spent making the spec precise pays off more than time spent watching the implementation.

techniques.name: Scope investigations narrowly; delegate research to subagents
techniques.description: The 'infinite exploration' anti-pattern: an unscoped 'investigate X' prompt makes Claude read hundreds of files and balloon the main context. Fix: scope the request to specific files/symptoms, or delegate to a subagent that explores in a separate context window and reports back only a summary, keeping the main conversation clean for implementation. Anthropic also notes RAG/index-based code search can be stale ('reflects the codebase as it previously existed'); agentic live search works but needs enough starting context to know where to look.

techniques.name: Manage context aggressively: /clear between tasks, checkpoint long sessions
techniques.description: Two named failure patterns: the 'kitchen sink session' (one task, then an unrelated one, then back — context full of noise) and 'correcting over and over' (context polluted with failed approaches). Anthropic's rule: /clear between unrelated tasks, and after two failed corrections on the same issue, /clear and write a better initial prompt incorporating what you learned — a clean session with a better prompt almost always beats a long session with accumulated corrections. Practitioners add: checkpoint every 45-60 minutes and persist progress in plan/context/tasks files so a post-compaction 'continue' reloads state without re-explaining.

techniques.name: Keep diffs reviewable — but don't hard-code 'single-file only' as a permanent rule
techniques.description: Practitioners advocate one goal per change so diffs stay reviewable. Important conflict to flag: Anthropic's large-codebases guidance warns that a CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude to 'break every refactor into single-file changes may have helped an earlier model stay on track but would prevent a newer one from making coordinated cross-file edits.' The takeaway is not 'never make big diffs' but 'keep changes scoped to one intent and re-examine configs every 3-6 months or after major model releases' rather than freezing an old constraint.

techniques.name: Add an adversarial review step in a fresh context before calling it done
techniques.description: The model that wrote the code is biased toward it. Run a reviewer in a fresh subagent context that sees only the diff and the criteria (e.g. 'review the diff against PLAN.md; check every requirement is implemented and nothing outside scope changed; report gaps, not style'). Use the bundled /code-review skill for correctness, or a Writer/Reviewer two-session pattern. Caveat from the docs: a reviewer asked to find gaps will usually find some even when work is sound, leading to over-engineering — tell it to flag only gaps affecting correctness or stated requirements.

techniques.name: Prune CLAUDE.md — bloat causes Claude to ignore your actual rules
techniques.description: An over-long CLAUDE.md is a documented failure mode: 'Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions.' The diagnostic: if Claude keeps doing something despite a rule against it, the file is too long and the rule is getting lost. Fix: for each line ask 'would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?' and cut otherwise; move sometimes-relevant knowledge to skills (loaded on demand) and convert must-happen-every-time rules to deterministic hooks. The digitalapplied blog adds a specific (self-reported, not studied) heuristic that the model reads files in full under ~200 lines and 'samples' past ~500 — treat that figure as their claim rather than an established number.

techniques.name: Watch team-level anti-patterns: skill sprawl, permission drift, hook spam, agent-blame postmortems
techniques.description: Beyond a single session, team adoption fails in characteristic ways per the digitalapplied audit: skill sprawl (library grows but most entries never invoked — 'curation is the work; collection is the trap'), permission drift (settings.json allow-lists grow 'like a geological record' with entries from departed engineers), hook spam (notification floods get filtered out, so even important events are ignored), and agent-blame postmortems (blaming model hallucination instead of the missing human-side controls — review, scope, permissions). Corrective theme: treat skills/subagents/permissions as production artifacts with named owners and quarterly review. Note these specific figures are one blog's self-reported metrics, not independent study results.
